Then the ayah adds *lā rayba fīh*, "wherein there is no doubt," *min rabbi'l-ʿālamīn*, "from the Lord of all that exists." Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion himself: "With this complete and more than sufficient explanation, the Qur'an leaves no doubt that it is from Allah, the Lord of all that exists." The completeness of the explanation is itself part of what removes the doubt.

## Ayah 38: the challenge

*Am yaqūlūna'ftarāh* — "Or do they say: 'He has forged it?'" The Qur'an states their charge in their own words, then hands them the means to prove it: *qul fa'tū bi-sūratin mithlih*, "Say: 'Bring then a Surah like unto it.'"

Ibn Kathir spells out the reasoning. "If you argue, claim and doubt whether this is from Allah then you uttered a lie and blasphemy, and you say it is from Muhammad ﷺ — Muhammad ﷺ, however, is a man like you, and since he came as you claim with this Qur'an — then you produce a Surah like one of its Surahs." So the challenge takes the accusation seriously on its own terms: if a man of your own kind produced this, a man of your own kind can produce its like. Not the whole Book. One surah. And you need not work alone: *wa'dʿū mani'stataʿtum min dūni'llāh* — "and call upon whomsoever you can besides Allah." Ibn Kathir: "Produce something of the same nature and seek help and support with all the power you have from humans and Jinns."

There is a quiet symmetry between the two ayat worth pausing on. The phrase *min dūni'llāh*, "other than Allah," stands in both. In ayah 37 it denies that anyone other than Allah could have produced this. In ayah 38 the deniers are invited to call on everyone other than Allah to help them try. Humans and jinn together are offered as collaborators — and Ibn Kathir says the outcome was announced in advance: "He told them that they would not be able to do it. They would have no way of doing so."

**The challenge came in stages.** Ibn Kathir lays them out. First: "Say: 'If the mankind and the Jinn were together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like thereof, even if they helped one another'" (17:88). "Then He reduced the number for them to ten Surahs similar to it, in the beginning of Surah Hud": "Bring you then ten forged Surah like unto it, and call whomsoever you can, other than Allah, if you speak the truth!" (11:13). Then, in this surah, He "went even further to challenge them to produce only one Surah" (10:38) — Ibn Kathir calls this "the third stage." And in Sūrat al-Baqarah, which he notes is "a Madinite Surah," the challenge to produce one surah comes with the verdict attached in advance: "But if you do it not, and you can never do it, then fear the Fire" (2:24).

Read the sequence and see how far the demand was lowered — from the whole Qur'an, to ten surahs, to one — while the invitation to bring help stands unchanged at every stage: call whomsoever you can besides Allah. As Ibn Kathir puts it, "Allah even suggested that they seek help from anyone they chose."

## Why the test was eloquence

Ibn Kathir makes a point here that turns the challenge from an abstract dare into something you can feel. "Eloquence was a part of the nature and character of the Arabs. Arabic poetry including Al-Muʿallaqāt — the oldest complete collection of the most eloquent ancient Arabic poems — was considered to be the best in the literary arts." Into that culture, he says, "Allah sent down to them something whose style none were familiar with, and no one is equal in stature to imitate."

That is why the earliest believers believed. Ibn Kathir: "those who believed among them, believed because of what they knew and felt in the Book, including its beauty, elegance, benefit, and fluency. They became the most knowledgeable of the Qur'an and its best in adhering to it." The people best equipped to judge were the ones who submitted — and their recognition did not stop at admiration. It turned into knowledge and into practice.

**The same pattern with earlier prophets.** Ibn Kathir sets two parallels beside it. The magicians in the time of Firʿawn "were knowledgeable of the arts of sorcery"; when Mūsā (peace be upon him) performed his miracles, "they knew that it must have come through someone that was supported and guided by Allah. They knew that no human could perform such acts without the permission of Allah." And ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) "was sent at the time of scholarly medicine and during the advancement in the treatment of patients. He healed the blind, lepers and raised the dead to life by Allah's leave" — something "no form of treatment or medicine could reproduce," so that those who believed in him "knew that he was Allah's servant and His Messenger."

Ibn Kathir presents these as one recurring pattern: the sign came into the field where the people's own expertise lay, and those best placed to detect a fake were the first to know it was not one.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith reported in the Sahih, in which Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "There was never a Prophet but he was given signs by which the people would recognize him, and that which I was given is revelation that Allah revealed, so I hope that I will have the most followers among them."

Sit with the contrast the hadith itself draws. Other prophets were given signs by which their people would recognise them. What he ﷺ was given is revelation that Allah revealed — and it is on that basis that he expresses the hope of having the most followers. The sign is the Book, and the Book is what is in your hands, still making the same offer ayah 38 made.

## Ayah 39: rejecting what you have not yet grasped

*Bal kadhdhabū bimā lam yuḥīṭū bi-ʿilmih* — "Nay, they have belied the knowledge whereof they could not comprehend." Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and exact: "They did not believe in the Qur'an and they have not yet grasped it or comprehended it."

So the verdict came before the understanding. They passed judgment on a Book they had not comprehended, and Ibn Kathir's summary is blunt: "they belied it out of ignorance and foolishness."

The ayah adds *wa lammā ya'tihim ta'wīluh* — "and what has not yet been fulfilled." Ibn Kathir explains this of them: "They have not attained the guidance and the true religion."

**The precedent.** *Kadhālika kadhdhaba'lladhīna min qablihim* — "Thus those before them did belie," meaning, says Ibn Kathir, "the past nations." Then: *fa'nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu'ẓ-ẓālimīn*, "Then see what was the end of the wrongdoers!" Ibn Kathir reads this as a direct warning: "Look at how we Destroyed them because they denied Our Messengers in their wickedness, pride, stubbornness and ignorance. So beware you who deny the message that the same end will befall you." The command is *unẓur* — look. The history is not decoration; it is set in front of you and you are told to examine it.

## Ayah 40: two responses, and a Lord who knows

*Wa minhum man yu'minu bihi wa minhum man lā yu'minu bih* — "And of them there are some who believe therein; and of them there are some who believe not therein." Ibn Kathir: among those you were sent to, O Muhammad ﷺ, "are people who will believe in this Qur'an, follow you and benefit from what has been sent to you," while the other "dies as a disbeliever and will be resurrected as such."

This is honest comfort for the Prophet ﷺ. A proof this clear will still not sweep everyone along. The split is stated in advance, before it happens.

Then: *wa rabbuka aʿlamu bi'l-mufsidīn* — "And your Lord is All-Aware of the mischief-makers." The passage does not close with human argument; it closes with divine knowledge. Ibn Kathir: "He best knows those who deserve guidance, so He guides them, and those who deserve to go astray, He allows to go astray. Allah is, however, the Just who is never unjust. He gives everyone what they deserve. All Glory is His, the Exalted."

Guidance and misguidance are in Allah's hand, and His dealing is perfect justice — "He gives everyone what they deserve." That is exactly how the passage means to leave us: certain about the Book, and leaving the hearts of others to the One who knows them.

## Living it

**Do not pass judgment on what you have not understood.** Ayah 39 names the failure precisely: they belied what they had "not yet grasped" or comprehended, and Ibn Kathir calls that ignorance and foolishness. The same instinct is alive in anyone who dismisses a verse, a ruling, or a whole religion on the strength of a headline. Study first, verdict after.

**Let the Book itself be the argument.** The first believers, Ibn Kathir says, believed because of what they "knew and felt in the Book, including its beauty, elegance, benefit, and fluency." That door is not closed. Slow recitation, real attention to the words, learning enough Arabic to feel the phrasing — this is the route by which the earliest believers arrived. And note where it took them: "They became the most knowledgeable of the Qur'an and its best in adhering to it." Knowledge and practice rose together.

**Expect the split, and stay steady.** Ayah 40 prepares you for the fact that clear proof does not guarantee acceptance. Present the truth plainly, and leave the hearts to the One who is All-Aware of them.

**Take the warning seriously.** *Fa'nẓur* — look at how it ended for those who denied. Ibn Kathir turns that from ancient history into a personal address: "So beware you who deny the message that the same end will befall you."

passages.title: If they deny you: the deaf and the blind
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the Prophet's ﷺ instructions for the moment when the argument is finished and the denial still stands. Ayah 41 gives him the words to say; ayat 42 and 43 explain why such words became necessary — there were people listening to him and watching him closely, and none of it was reaching them; ayah 44 forecloses the objection that this outcome is somehow unfair to them. Together they move from a stance to take, to a diagnosis of why the stance is needed, to the justice of Allah that underwrites the whole thing.

## The backdrop: after the truth, only error

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to what the surah had already settled a few ayat earlier, in ayah 32: *"So, that is Allah, your Lord in truth. And what is there, after truth, but error?"* This is the Sacred Being whose attributes of perfection had just been mentioned. Once you have found the truth, there remains nothing else to find except error and straying. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, once it stands proved that Allah alone is the true and rightful object of worship, it is terribly senseless to abandon that truth and allow yourself to be diverted elsewhere.

That statement, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, also establishes a point of creed: **there is no intermediary link between truth and error.** What is not the truth will be included in error and straying — there can be no such thing that is neither truth nor error, and it is not possible that two opposite things could both be the truth. This is an established rule in the sight of the majority of scholars in the Muslim Ummah. Hold that in mind, because it is exactly why ayah 41 draws such a clean line. When two paths cannot both be right, the only honest thing left to do is to say plainly which one you are on.

## Ayah 41: "My deeds are mine"

The ayah opens with a condition — *if they deny you*, if they treat what you have brought as a lie. Ibn Kathir renders it: *and if they belie you*. It is a verdict pronounced on the Prophet ﷺ.

The answer he is given is not an argument. It is a separation. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah said to His Prophet ﷺ: *if these idolators belie you, then be clear from them and their deeds.* **"Say: For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do."**

That is the language of a clean break: your account is yours, mine is mine, and neither of us is answerable for the other's.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two other passages where the same disavowal is spoken:

- *"Say: O you disbelievers! I worship not that which you worship"* (109:1–2), to the end of that surah.
- **Ibrahim Al-Khalil (the Friend) and his followers**, who said to the idolators among their people: *"Verily, we are free from you and whatever you worship besides Allah"* (60:4).

Notice what that comparison establishes. This stance is not something new. It had already been spoken by Ibrahim and those with him to the idolators among their people. And notice the terms in which each disavowal is framed: what one worships, and what one does. The Prophet ﷺ is told to be clear of *them and their deeds* — to stop carrying what is not his to carry.

**One important limit.** Because this ayah is often reached for too quickly, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's qualification is worth keeping beside it. The rule that what is not truth is error is stated in relation to issues of religious belief. Regarding minor and subsidiary juristic issues, difference exists among the ʿUlamaʼ: in the view of some, both sides would be considered as upon truth in *ijtihad*-based issues (*ijtihad* being a qualified scholar's reasoned effort to derive a ruling), and according to the majority there is consensus that taking the contra-position in an ijtihad-based problem cannot be termed error and straying. The line drawn in ayah 41 is the line around worship — Allah alone as the true and rightful object of worship, as against what is worshipped besides Him. It is not a template for disowning a Muslim who reached a different conclusion on a subsidiary question of fiqh.

## Ayat 42–43: two doors, both shut

Having given the instruction, Allah now shows why it was needed — and He does it by taking the two ordinary routes by which a proof reaches a person, and showing both of them blocked.

**The ears (ayah 42):** *"And among them are some who listen to you."* These were not people at the back of the crowd who missed it. They were listening.

And what were they listening to? Ibn Kathir's description is worth reading slowly: **They listen to your beautiful talk and to the Glorious Qurʼan. They listen to your truthful, eloquent and authentic Hadiths that are useful to the hearts, the bodies and their faith.** He then says something striking — *this is indeed a great benefit and is sufficient.* The material was more than enough. What was offered to their ears could benefit a heart, a body, and a faith. The failure was not in what reached them.

**The eyes (ayah 43):** *"And among them are some who look at you."* Here the proof is not the message but the messenger. Ibn Kathir explains: they look at you, and at **what Allah has given you in terms of dignity, noble personality and great conduct** — and there is in all of this clear evidence of your prophethood *to those who have reason and insight*. The life of the Prophet ﷺ was itself an argument, visible to anyone with eyes.

But, he continues, other people also look and do not receive guidance like them. In his words: **"Believers look at you with respect and dignity while disbelievers regard you with contempt."** The same man, the same conduct, two opposite verdicts — because what a person sees depends on what he brings to the looking. Ibn Kathir cites how far that contempt could go: *"And when they see you, they treat you only in mockery"* (25:41).

**The two questions.** To each of these Allah puts a question back to His Prophet ﷺ: *"but can you make the deaf to hear"* and *"can you guide the blind"*. The question is addressed to him — the one who was doing all the delivering. Ibn Kathir states the conclusion plainly: **guiding the people to the truth is not up to you or to them. You cannot make the deaf hear. Therefore you cannot guide these people except if Allah wishes.**

**Why "even though."** Neither ayah stops at the outer faculty. Ayah 42 does not merely say they are deaf; it adds *"even though they apprehend not."* Ayah 43 does not merely say they are blind; it adds *"even though they see not."* The inner faculty is named alongside the outer one. This is precisely why Ibn Kathir could say the visible evidence of prophethood was clear *to those who have reason and insight* — where reason and insight had gone, the equipment for receiving a proof had gone with them.

## Ayah 44: and yet Allah has wronged no one

If guidance rests with Allah, the objection writes itself: then how is any of this their fault? Ayah 44 answers before the question is finished. **"Truly, Allah wrongs not mankind in aught; but mankind wrong themselves."**

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here announces that He is never unjust with anyone. **He guides whomever He wills and opens the eyes of the blind, makes the deaf hear and removes neglect from the hearts. At the same time He lets others go astray, moving away from faith.** He does all of that yet He is always Just, for He is the Ruler and has full authority over His kingdom. He does whatever He wills without any restrictions. No one can question Him as to what He does, while He will question everyone else. He is Omniscient, All-Wise, and All-Just.

Two truths are held together here without either being softened. Guidance is genuinely in Allah's hand — the opening of blind eyes and the making of the deaf to hear are His acts, not the preacher's achievement and not the listener's entitlement. And the wrong done is genuinely the person's own: *mankind wrong themselves.* The ayah does not resolve the tension by taking away Allah's authority over His kingdom, nor by taking away human responsibility. It states both, and adds a third thing: whatever He does, injustice is not in it.

Note carefully how the ayah says it. Allah does not wrong people *in aught* — not in the least, not by the smallest thing. And yet the wronging in the sentence has not disappeared; it has changed hands. It comes back at the end of the ayah with the people as the ones doing it — and with themselves as the ones it is done to.

## From the Sunnah

For this ayah, Ibn Kathir brings the hadith narrated by **Abu Dharr**, in which the Prophet ﷺ related that his Lord, Exalted and High is He, said:

> **"O My servant! I have prohibited oppression for Myself and made it prohibited for you, so do not oppress one another..."**

and, at the end of the same hadith:

> **"O My servants! It is but your deeds that I reckon for you and then recompense you for. So let him who finds good (in the Hereafter) praise Allah. And let him who finds other than that blame no one but himself."**

Ibn Kathir notes that the complete version was recorded by **Muslim**.

This is the ayah's own commentary, spoken by the Prophet ﷺ from his Lord. First, oppression is something Allah has prohibited for His own Self. Set that beside what Ibn Kathir had just said — that no one can question Him as to what He does — and see what we have been given: the One with full authority over His kingdom has told us Himself what He will not do.

Second, look at the closing line and then look again at ayah 41. There the Prophet ﷺ was told to say, *"For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds."* Here Allah says, *"It is but your deeds that I reckon for you and then recompense you for."* The separation the Prophet ﷺ was told to declare in this world is the same separation that will be enacted when the deeds are reckoned. Nobody's account will be mixed with anyone else's. Whoever finds good praises Allah — and Ibn Kathir has already told us whose act it is to guide, and to open the eyes of the blind. Whoever finds other than that blames no one but himself.

## Living it

**For anyone who calls to Allah.** These ayat lift a weight that was never yours. Your responsibility is the delivering — the beautiful talk, the Qurʼan, the sound teaching that is useful to hearts and bodies and faith, and the conduct that is itself an argument. Ibn Kathir called that a great benefit and *sufficient*. The opening of a heart is not on your list of duties: guiding people to the truth, he says, is not up to you. When someone you love listens attentively and walks away unchanged, ayah 42 is telling you that this happened in front of the Prophet ﷺ himself, with the Qurʼan in his mouth. Grief over it is right; guilt over it is misplaced.

**On disassociation.** Ayah 41 is a stance about worship and deeds, stated in those terms — not a licence for contempt. The Prophet ﷺ was told to be clear of them and their deeds and to stop owning what was not his; the mockery recorded in 25:41 came from their side, not his.

**On yourself.** The most searching use of these ayat is inward. Ask which listening is yours: the listening of those who came to hear him, or the hearing that lets the words pass through. Ask what you see when you look at the Prophet ﷺ — the dignity, noble personality and great conduct that Ibn Kathir says are clear evidence to those who have reason and insight, or something you are quick to dismiss. The deafness and blindness described here come paired with a failure to apprehend and a failure to see.

**And when the accounting comes.** Do not fear injustice from Allah — He has prohibited oppression for Himself, and He does not wrong people in the least. Fear what you have done to yourself. That fear is useful, because the door is still open: the One who opens the eyes of the blind and makes the deaf hear is the same One you can ask.

passages.title: The gathering, the messenger, the just verdict
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Three ayat, one scene: the gathering, the messenger, the just verdict. Ayah 45 shows us all people assembled, carrying with them the feeling that their whole stay lasted an hour. Ayah 46 tells the Prophet ﷺ that the reckoning does not depend on whether he lives to see it. Ayah 47 shows the verdict itself being handed down, with every community's own messenger standing there.

## Ayah 45 — a whole lifetime that felt like an hour

"And on the Day when He shall gather them together, (it will be) as if they had not stayed (in the life of this world and graves) but an hour of a day."

Ibn Kathir opens by naming the purpose of the ayah: Allah says this "to remind people of the establishment of the Hour and their resurrection from their graves to the gathering for the Day of Judgment."

The striking thing is not the crowd but the sensation the people carry with them. Everything they lived — and, as the translation notes, the stay in the graves as well — collapses in memory into "an hour of a day." Not a day. An hour *out of* a day: a fragment of a fragment.

Ibn Kathir then does something worth noticing. Rather than explaining this feeling, he lets the Qur'an say it again and again until the reader feels it:

- "On the Day when they will see that (torment) with which they are promised, (it will be) as if they had not stayed more than an hour in a single day." (46:35)
- "The Day they see it, (it will be) as if they had not tarried (in this world) except an afternoon or a morning." (79:46)
- "The Day when the Trumpet will be blown: that Day, We shall gather the criminals, blue eyed. They will speak in a very low voice to each other (saying): 'You stayed not longer than ten (days).' We know very well what they will say, when the best among them in knowledge and wisdom will say: 'You stayed no longer than a day!'" (20:102–104)
- "And on the Day that the Hour will be established, the criminals will swear that they stayed not but an hour." (30:55)

Notice what that third passage puts side by side: some of them whisper "ten days," and the one the ayah calls "the best among them in knowledge and wisdom" says a single day. And in the final exchange Ibn Kathir cites, Allah Himself closes the argument:

"He will say: 'What number of years did you stay on earth?' They will say: 'We stayed a day or part of a day. Ask of those who keep account.' He will say: 'You stayed not but a little, if you had only known!'" (23:112–114)

Even their own answer wavers — "a day or part of a day" — and then they hand the question elsewhere: "Ask of those who keep account." Ibn Kathir's verdict on this whole chorus of ayat is one sentence: "These all are evidence of the brevity of the worldly life compared to the Hereafter."

That is the passage's first work on the heart. The ayah sets that brevity directly beside the ruin of "those who denied the meeting with Allah" — the very life that felt enormous and permanent turns out, from the other side of death, to have been an hour.

## "They will recognize each other" — the most human line in the passage

Then comes the phrase *yataʿārafūna baynahum* — "they will recognize each other."

Ibn Kathir describes it warmly: "The children will know their parents and relatives will recognize one another. They will know them just like they used to know them during the life in this world." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān makes the same point about the moment of rising: when the dead are raised from their graves, "they will recognize each other as if not much time had passed when they met last."

And then Ibn Kathir turns the knife, gently: "However, on that Day everyone will be busy with himself." He supports it with two ayat:

- "Then, when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them." (23:101)
- "And no friend will ask a friend (about his condition)." (70:10)

So the recognition is real and the relationship is useless. You will see the face of the person you loved most and have nothing to spend on them — no help, not even the ordinary courtesy of asking how they are. Recognition without rescue.

**Where the scholars differ on how long this lasts.** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān preserves two positions. Imām al-Baghawī held that this recognition belongs to the early stage; later, when the horrendous happenings of the Qiyāmah unfold, "this ability to recognize each other will stand disabled." According to some other narrations, reported there from Mazharī, the ability to recognize one another does still remain, but such will be the awe of the situation that they will be unable to say anything. Both readings arrive at the same silence: whether the faces blur or the tongues freeze, no one is coming to help.

## "Ruined indeed" — naming the loss precisely

The ayah ends: "Ruined indeed will be those who denied the meeting with Allah and were not guided." Ibn Kathir sets it beside "Woe that Day to the deniers" (77:15).

Two things are said about them. They **denied the meeting with Allah** — the refusal to believe there will ever be a day of accounting. And they **were not guided** — which is worth holding in mind, because ayah 47 will state that every community had a messenger.

Ibn Kathir defines the loss with unusual tenderness: "Woe to them because they will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. That is indeed the great loss. There is no loss greater than the loss of one who will be taken away from his dear ones on the Day of Grief and Regret." Loss here is not only punishment in the abstract. It is being separated, permanently, from the people you spent that "hour of a day" loving.

## Ayah 46 — a word of steadiness to the Prophet ﷺ

"Whether We show you some of what We promise them (the torment), or We cause you to die — still unto Us is their return, and moreover Allah is Witness over what they used to do."

Ibn Kathir heads this section: *The Criminals will certainly be avenged — whether in This World or in the Hereafter.* The Prophet ﷺ is addressed directly and given two possibilities with one outcome.

**Possibility one:** "Whether We show you some of what We promise them." Ibn Kathir explains: "We shall avenge them in your lifetime so your eye will be delighted." And note the wording of the ayah itself: *some* of what is promised, not all of it.

**Possibility two:** "Or We cause you to die — still unto Us is their return." If he ﷺ does not live to see it, nothing is lost from the account, because the account was never his to keep. "Allah will then be the Witness watching over their actions for you," writes Ibn Kathir.

That is why the ayah closes as it does: **Allah is Witness over what they used to do.** Nothing they did has gone unseen, and nothing needs a human eye to confirm it.

There is a quiet mercy in this for anyone who has watched wrongdoing go unpunished. The ayah does not promise that you will see justice done. It promises that their return is to Allah, and that He has been Witness all along.

## Ayah 47 — every community, its own messenger, and the verdict

"And for every Ummah there is a Messenger; when their Messenger comes, the matter will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged."

**When does the messenger "come"?** Mujāhid said: "This will be on the Day of Resurrection." So the coming spoken of here is the messenger standing there on that Day — which is exactly the scene Ibn Kathir goes on to describe.

Ibn Kathir draws in "And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord" (39:69), and continues: "every nation will be presented before Allah in the presence of its Messenger and the Book of its deeds. All good and evil deeds will be witnessed upon them. Their guardian angels will be witnesses too. The nations will be brought forth, one by one."

Look at what that courtroom contains: the community itself, its messenger present before Allah, the Book of its deeds, and the guardian angels as witnesses. Nothing is missing. And the nations are brought "one by one" — not a single mass verdict, but each community brought forward in turn.

**"With justice — and they will not be wronged."** The verdict is passed *bil-qisṭ*, with justice, and then the ayah adds the assurance in its own words: *they will not be wronged*. Not even the deniers whose ruin ayah 45 announced.

And notice how the messenger completes the justice. Ayah 45 spoke of those who "were not guided"; ayah 47 states that guidance had been sent — "for every Ummah there is a Messenger" — and that each community stands before Allah with that very messenger present. The evidence and the accused are in the same place.

## From the Sunnah: the last nation judged first

Ibn Kathir adds an honour that belongs to this ummah specifically: although it is the last of the nations, it is the first on the Day of Resurrection to be questioned and judged. He cites a hadith recorded by both Al-Bukhari and Muslim, in which Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "We are the last, the first on the Day of Resurrection. We will be judged before the rest of the creatures."

And Ibn Kathir is careful about *why*: "His Ummah attains the honor of precedence only by the honor of its Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him forever, until the Day of Judgement." The precedence is not earned by our numbers or our era. It is borrowed light — it comes from him ﷺ.

## Living it

The passage asks for three adjustments, and they follow one from the other.

**Price this life correctly.** You will one day describe your entire life as "an hour of a day," and you will not be exaggerating. Ibn Kathir says plainly why Allah gathers all these ayat together: they are "evidence of the brevity of the worldly life compared to the Hereafter," said in order "to remind people of the establishment of the Hour." The reminder is meant to land now, while it can still change something. Every decision about time, wealth and delay looks different when the unit of measurement is an hour rather than decades.

**Do not bank on people.** You will recognise them; you will not be helped by them. No kinship, no friend asking after a friend. Since you cannot rescue them on that Day either, use this hour to bring the people you love toward guidance rather than assuming you will stand together by default.

**Leave the verdict with Allah.** Ayah 46 taught the Prophet ﷺ himself that he might not live to see the promise fall, and that this changes nothing — "still unto Us is their return." If that consolation was enough for him ﷺ, it is enough for us. Our work is the message and the deed; the judging is Allah's, and it will be exact — "and they will not be wronged."

passages.title: "When will this threat come?" The appointed term
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** The idolators who rejected the Message taunt the believers: *when* is this threat of yours going to arrive? These six ayat answer them — not with a date, but by dismantling the question itself. What holds ayat 48–53 together is a single movement: a mocking demand for timing (48), the Prophet's ﷺ answer that timing is not his to give and that every community has a fixed term (49), a question turned back on the mockers about what exactly they are in a hurry for (50), the shutting of the door of faith at the moment the punishment lands (51), the sentence pronounced (52), and an oath sworn by the Lord Himself in answer to those who deny the return (53).

## The question that was never a real question

Ayah 48 reports their words: *"When will this threat come to pass, if you are truthful?"* Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us about the idolators who reject faith through their demand that the punishment be hastened, inquiring about the *time* of it. His remark on their motive is worth pausing over: **the response to such a question is not inherently beneficial, yet they inquired anyway.** Knowing the date would not have made them better people. The question was a weapon, not a search.

Ibn Kathir sets their attitude beside another ayah: *"Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it, while those who believe are fearful of it, and know that it is the very truth"* (42:18). Two hearts hear the same announcement. One says "bring it on"; the other trembles. And notice what the believers have that the mockers do not — not information, but certainty. As Ibn Kathir puts it, they know it is the truth because it is definitely going to happen; it is going to take place **even if they have no idea when it will occur.** The believer's confidence was never resting on a calendar.

## "I have no power over harm or benefit for myself"

The reply in ayah 49 is startling for how little it claims. Allah does not tell His Messenger ﷺ to answer with a display of authority. He tells him to say: *"I have no power to benefit or protect myself, except what Allah wills."*

Ibn Kathir unfolds the sense in the Prophet's ﷺ own voice: *I will not say except what He has taught me. I also have no authority over anything that Allah has not shown to me. I am Allah's servant and His Messenger to you.* Then the decisive line: **"I was told that the Hour is going to come, but He has not told me when it will occur."**

Sit with that. The very Messenger they are pressing for a date is instructed to say plainly that this particular knowledge was not given to him. Prophethood is not autonomy. A messenger transmits what he is given and stops where the giving stops. The same statement appears again in the Qur'an at 7:188 — a servant who says he cannot secure benefit or ward off harm for *himself* except as Allah wills. If he says he owns nothing of that for his own person, the demand that he hurry along a punishment collapses on the ayah's own logic.

## Ajal: the term nobody moves

Having declined to give a date, the ayah gives something better — a law. *"For every Ummah, there is a term appointed."*

The word is **ajal** — an appointed term, a fixed end-point set in advance. Ibn Kathir explains it here as meaning that **for every generation or community there is a set term appointed for them**; and when the end of that term approaches, *"neither can they delay it nor can they advance it an hour."* The Arabic word rendered "an hour" is *sāʿah* — Ibn Kathir's text glosses it "an hour (or a moment)" — not merely a long postponement but the smallest slippage in either direction.

He then places the communal law beside its individual twin: *"And Allah grants respite to none when his appointed time comes"* (63:11) — a verse Ibn Kathir's text glosses as being about death. What is true of a nation is true of a person. Your *ajal* is not negotiable and not knowable, which means the mockers' demand is doubly futile: they cannot pull the appointment forward by asking for it, and they will not push it back by refusing to believe in it. The clock is not theirs.

## Night or day — and what exactly are you hurrying?

Ibn Kathir introduces the next ayah with a single word for the whole matter: Allah instructed His Messenger ﷺ to tell the people that His punishment would come **suddenly**. Ayah 50: *"Tell me — if His torment should come to you by night or by day, which portion thereof would the criminals hasten on?"*

Two things are doing work here. First, *bayātan aw nahāran*, "by night or by day." Whether it arrives in the dark while they sleep or in daylight while they trade, they will not have chosen the hour — which is exactly what Ibn Kathir means by "suddenly," and exactly why asking for a schedule is pointless.

Second, the question *"which portion thereof would the criminals hasten on?"* is devastating in its calm. Of this thing you are demanding — which part, exactly, are you eager for? Say the words back to yourself and the bravado dies. Ayah 50 does not argue with them; it simply asks them to look at what they are asking for.

## "Now?" — the door that closes

Ayah 51 is where the passage turns: *"Will you believe in it only after it has overtaken you? Now?"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as: would you believe when the Divine punishment is actually descending upon you — whether at the time of death, or even before it? And at that moment the response to your believing will be **آلْآنَ** *(al-ān:* "now?"). Meaning, as Maʿārif puts it: is it *now* that you have come to believe, **while the time of believing has already passed?**

One syllable of Arabic carries the entire tragedy. It is not a question requesting information. It is the sound of a door being shut.

Ibn Kathir shows what that moment sounds like from the inside. When the punishment befalls them they will say: *"Our Lord! We have now seen and heard"* (32:12). And: *"So when they saw Our punishment, they said: 'We believe in Allah alone and reject all that we used to associate with Him as partners.' Then their faith could not avail them when they saw Our punishment. Like this has been the way of Allah in dealing with His servants. And there the disbelievers lost utterly"* (40:84–85). Note the phrase — **the way of Allah** with His servants. This is not a mood or an exception; it is a settled pattern in how Allah deals with people.

### Pharaoh, and the exact edge of repentance

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a parallel that makes this concrete, and it comes from later in this very surah. Pharaoh, drowning, said: *"I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit"* (10:90). The answer he received was the same word: *آلْآنَ* — "now?" **His believing was not accepted.**

Maʿārif then cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah keeps accepting the repentance of His servant until he is seized by the agony of death. (Maʿārif quotes the teaching without naming a collection, so no collection can be named here.) The ruling Maʿārif draws from it: believing and repenting at the time of the agony of death is not credible in the sight of Allah. And the same principle governs punishment in this world — repentance can be accepted **before** the punishment actually falls; once it strikes, it is not accepted.

Then comes the counter-example, and Maʿārif tells us the event is coming towards the end of this same surah: the people of Sayyidnā Yūnus, whose repentance was accepted. They fall under this very rule, not outside it. **They had seen the punishment coming from a distance** — it had not yet struck. Moved earnestly, weeping and wailing, they made their repentance in all sincerity, and the punishment was withdrawn. Maʿārif states the boundary exactly: had it struck them, their repentance would have remained unaccepted.

So the mercy in this passage is enormous and it is precise. The window is open the entire length of your life. On Maʿārif's rule it closes at two points: when the punishment actually falls, and when the agony of death takes hold. Everything before that is still inside the window — including today.

## The sentence (ayah 52)

*"Then the wrongdoers will be told: Taste the torment of eternity! Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?"*

Ibn Kathir renders the opening as *"Then it will be said to them who wronged themselves,"* and says this will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection **blaming and rebuking them**. He brings the parallel scene: *"The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing. This is the Fire that you used to belie. Is this magic, or do you not see? Taste you therein its heat; and whether you are patient of it or impatient of it, it is all the same. You are only being requited for what you used to do"* (52:13–16).

Hold ayah 52 against ayah 51 and the shape of it lands. They had been hastening it on; what they receive is *ʿadhāb al-khuld*, "the torment of eternity." And the closing question — *are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?* — forecloses any complaint of injustice, exactly as the parallel ayah does: *you are only being requited for what you used to do.* Nothing has been added to their account.

## "Yes — by my Lord!" (ayah 53)

Ayah 53 shifts register. Now they come asking to be *informed*: *"Is this true?"* Ibn Kathir explains that they are asking about the return and the Resurrection from the graves — **after the bodies become sand**.

The answer is an oath: *"Say: Yes! By my Lord! It is the very truth! And you cannot escape it."*

Ibn Kathir's reply to the objection is one sentence: *"you cannot escape it"* means **that becoming sand does not make Allah incapable of bringing you back, since He originated you from nothing.** He follows it with: *"Verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is"* (36:82).

Notice that the objection was about bodies dissolving, and the answer is about Allah's power — not about how the dust might be reassembled. And the *ajal* of ayah 49 finds its counterpart here: an appointment that could not be moved forward or back is also one that cannot be escaped.

**A rare thing in the Qur'an.** Ibn Kathir points out that Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to give an oath by Him in answer to those who deny the return, and that there are only two other ayat in the Qur'an similar to this one. In Sūrah Sabaʾ: *"Those who disbelieve say: 'The Hour will not come to us.' Say: 'Yes, by my Lord, it will come to you'"* (34:3). And in Sūrat at-Taghābun: *"The disbelievers claimed that they will never be resurrected. Say: 'Yes! By my Lord, you will certainly be resurrected, then you will be informed of what you did; and that is easy for Allah'"* (64:7). Three places in the whole Book — and, as Ibn Kathir's own framing shows, all three are answering the denial of the return and the Hour. Ibn Kathir does not tell us why the oath is reserved for this subject; he tells us that it is. What the reader is left holding is the Messenger's ﷺ sworn word, staked on his Lord.

## Living it

**Stop asking the question the deniers asked.** Ibn Kathir's observation about ayah 48 is a mirror we can hold up to ourselves: the answer to their question would not have benefited them, and they asked anyway. Curiosity about the date of the Hour is that kind of question — Allah withheld it even from His Messenger ﷺ, who was told the Hour is coming but not told when.

**Take the *ajal* seriously.** Not one hour forward, not one hour back — for a community or for a person. And Ibn Kathir's word for how the punishment arrives is *suddenly*.

**Do not gamble on the last minute.** Pharaoh said the words of faith as he was drowning, and the answer was "now?" — his believing was not accepted. The people of Yūnus repented while the punishment was still at a distance, before it struck, and it was withdrawn. Maʿārif's rule is a rule about timing: repentance is accepted before the punishment actually falls; once it strikes, it is not.

**And hear the oath as it was meant.** *"Yes, by my Lord — it is the very truth."* The believer's response to a promise sworn to by the Messenger ﷺ in his Lord's name is not to demand a timetable, but to live as someone who already knows it is coming.

passages.title: No ransom on the Day of regret
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat bring a long argument to its close. The deniers had demanded to know whether the Resurrection was really going to happen; Allah answers with an oath, and then lets them see the moment when their question will be settled and nothing will be left to bargain with. What holds ayat 54–56 together is one movement: a desperate offer that will be made (54), the reason it can never be accepted (55), and the One before whom it is made — who gives life, takes it, and receives everyone back (56).

## The ransom nobody can pay (ayah 54)

**وَلَوۡ أَنَّ لِكُلِّ نَفۡسٖ ظَلَمَتۡ مَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ لَٱفۡتَدَتۡ بِهِۦ** — "And if every person who had wronged possessed all that is on the earth, and sought to ransom himself therewith…"

To feel the weight of this, you need the question it answers. Immediately before it stands ayah 53: **"And they ask you to inform them (saying): 'Is it true?'"** Ibn Kathir explains what they were asking about — "the return and the Resurrection from the graves, after the bodies become sand." That was their objection in a sentence: a body that has crumbled into dust cannot be reassembled.

The reply the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to give is startling: **"Say: 'Yes! By my Lord! It is the very truth! And you cannot escape it!'"** Ibn Kathir meets the objection head-on — becoming sand "does not make Allah incapable of bringing you back, since He originated you from nothing" — and cites the principle behind it: *"Verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is"* (36:82). He also notes that here Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ **to give an oath by Him** in answer to those who deny the return, and that there are only two other ayat in the Qur'an similar to this: *"Say: 'Yes, by my Lord! it will come to you'"* (34:3), and *"Say: 'Yes! By my Lord! you will certainly be resurrected'"* (64:7). All three are about the same denial. That tells you what kind of doubt this is — not a gap in the evidence, but a refusal that has to be met with the weight of an oath.

Ayah 54 then shows what that refusal costs. Look carefully at how the offer is described. It is not that the wrongdoers, between them, own the earth — it is that **every single person who wronged** possesses all that is on the earth. Each one, separately, with the whole planet in his hand. Ibn Kathir puts the scale in an image: on that Day the disbelievers "will wish that they could ransom themselves from Allah's punishment with the equivalent of the weight of the earth in gold."

And notice what the ayah does **not** say. The sentence simply hangs there: *if he had all that… he would offer it as ransom.* The refusal is not spelled out; Ibn Kathir has to supply it in brackets — *(it will not be accepted)*. The Qur'an leaves the offer unanswered, and then answers it in the next ayah.

## Regret kept inside

**وَأَسَرُّوا۟ ٱلنَّدَامَةَ لَمَّا رَأَوُا۟ ٱلۡعَذَابَ** — "and they would feel in their hearts regret when they see the torment."

Two details carry this half of the verse. First, the trigger: **when they see the torment**. The certainty they refused to accept finally arrives — by sight, at the last possible moment, when it can no longer change anything.

Second, where the regret sits. It is regret **felt in the heart** — inward, unspoken, with nowhere to go. It is not a plea that changes an outcome; it is what is left of a person after the outcome has already been decided.

**And then justice.** The ayah ends: *"and they will be judged with justice, and no wrong will be done unto them."* The refusal of the ransom is not cruelty — the same sentence insists the judgement is exact and measured, and that **no wrong will be done unto them**. Everything they receive that Day is a just reckoning; not one grain more is added.

## Why the offer fails (ayah 55)

**أَلَآ إِنَّ لِلَّهِ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ** — "No doubt, surely, all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah. No doubt, surely, Allah's promise is true. But most of them know not."

Here is the answer the previous ayah withheld. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: **"Allah is the Owner of the heavens and earth."** The ransom in ayah 54 was *all that is on the earth*. Ayah 55 answers with *all that is in the heavens **and** the earth*. The bid is not merely too small; it was never the bidder's property to offer. He would be handing Allah what already belongs to Allah, out of a world that is already His. That is why no price can be named.

Notice, too, how the ayah is built. The same opening — *"No doubt, surely"* — lands twice in a single verse: once on His ownership, and once on His promise, which as Ibn Kathir says **"is true and is indeed going to be fulfilled."** Then the sober close: *but most of them know not.* The problem was never a shortage of proof. It was that most of them did not know — and the verse is calling for exactly the attention they failed to give.

## The One you are returning to (ayah 56)

**هُوَ يُحۡيِۦ وَيُمِيتُ وَإِلَيۡهِ تُرۡجَعُونَ** — "It is He Who gives life, and causes death, and to Him you all shall return."

This closes the circle back to the objection about bodies becoming sand. Ibn Kathir's comment answers on two fronts at once: Allah "is the One Who gives life and causes death. To Him is the return of everyone, and He is the One who has the power over that, and the One Who knows everything about every creature; its deterioration, and where every speck of it has gone, be it land, oceans or otherwise."

Power and knowledge, together. Power, because the One who first gave life can give it again. Knowledge, because the objection assumed the dust gets lost — and Ibn Kathir insists that nothing is lost: every speck of every creature, wherever the land or the sea has taken it, is known to Him.

## When repentance is still accepted — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the timing that ayah 54 depends on, working from an earlier line of this sūrah — *"Would you believe when it actually happens? **Now?**"* Its explanation: would you believe only when the Divine punishment actually descends upon you, whether at death or before it? The answer given then will be one flat word: **now?** Is it now that you have come to believe, when the time for believing has already passed?

Maʿārif offers Pharaoh as the illustration — drowning, calling out: *"I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Isrāʾīl believe, and I am of the Muslims"* (10:90). The answer he received was that same word — **now?** — and, Maʿārif states, this believing by him was not accepted.

It then cites the Prophet ﷺ as having said that **Allah keeps accepting the repentance of His servant until he is seized by the agony of death**. (Maʿārif reports this simply as "In Hadith," without naming a collection, so it is passed on here the same way.) Believing and repenting once the death-agony has taken hold, the commentary explains, is not credible in the sight of Allah. The same rule applies in this world: repentance can be accepted before the punishment actually falls; once it strikes, it is not accepted.

And the hopeful side of that same rule is the counterweight this passage needs. **The people of Sayyidnā Yūnus**, whose story appears towards the end of this sūrah, *saw the punishment coming from a distance*. Moved earnestly, weeping and wailing, they made their repentance in all sincerity — and the punishment was withdrawn. Maʿārif is explicit that this falls under exactly the same principle: had the punishment already struck them, their repentance would have remained unaccepted. **The difference was not the sincerity. It was the timing.**

## What this asks of us

**Value your wealth by what it can still buy.** Ayah 54 names the precise moment at which every possession on earth becomes worthless — and by doing so it names the only time it is worth anything, which is now. What cannot ransom you then can be given away now, and that is the whole of its usefulness.

**Do not save regret for when it is useless.** The regret of ayah 54 arrives at the sight of the punishment, when nothing can be done with it. The same feeling, brought forward while the window is still open, is the very thing Allah is described as accepting right up until the agony of death takes hold. There is no wisdom in holding on to it.

**Give the verse the attention it asks for.** Ayah 55 does not end with "they were given no evidence." It ends with *most of them know not*. The ownership of the heavens and the earth, and the truth of Allah's promise, are each announced with an opening call to take notice — because what this passage diagnoses is not disproof but inattention.

**And keep ayah 56 in view.** He gives life; He causes death; to Him you are returned. Every one of those three is His, and only the middle stretch between them — this one — is where anything can be done about it.

passages.title: Revealed mercy versus self-made rulings
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These four ayat set two things side by side: what Allah has sent down to human beings out of sheer generosity, and what human beings have put up in its place out of their own invention. Ayat 57–58 describe the Qur'an as advice, cure, guidance and mercy, and tell people what is actually worth rejoicing over. Ayat 59–60 then cross-examine those same people about the rulings they had manufactured over Allah's own provision — declaring this lawful and that forbidden with no warrant from Him. The thread running through all four is **authority**: mercy comes down from the Lord, and the right to legislate belongs to Him, not to us.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the passage in its flow. The preceding verses had described how far the disbelievers and idolaters had strayed and what punishment had become due against them in the Hereafter. These two verses (57–58) then show them the way out of that error and the source through which they would find deliverance — the Qur'an, the Book of Allah, and His Messenger Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ. Both, it says, are blessings for humanity far superior to all the blessings of the heavens and the earth; following the Qur'an's injunctions and the way of the Prophet ﷺ makes a human being human in the real sense, and when a person becomes truly complete in this way, the whole world corrects and reorders itself like a paradise on earth.

## Ayah 57: four names for one gift

Notice first who is addressed — **"O humanity"** (*yā ayyuhā al-nās*), not "O you who believe". The offer is made to everyone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts four attributes of the Qur'an in this one ayah.

**1. Advice — *mawʿizah min rabbikum*.** The real sense of *mawʿizah* (and *waʿẓ*) is to lay out the sort of things that make a person's heart soft and receptive, so that it inclines towards Allah, so that the barrier of heedlessness built up by excessive indulgence in worldly life is removed, and so that it ends in a personal concern for what will happen in the Ākhirah — the life ahead. Ibn Kathir puts the same attribute in one line: it is "a warning and a shield from shameful deeds."

Maʿārif adds why the Qur'an does this so effectively. From beginning to end it is an eloquent preacher of exactly this counsel — everywhere you look there is promise paired with warning, reward paired with punishment, success in this world and the next set beside the fate that follows error and straying. Recurring in varying shades and blendings, it generates a powerful appeal that can take a heart hard as stone and make it soft and pliable as water, ready to absorb the message. And on top of everything there is the miraculous diction of the Qur'an itself, which is in a class of its own in the matter of turning hearts around.

Then look at the phrase **"from your Lord"**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this complement lifts the status of the advice to an altogether higher level. This counsel is not coming from some helpless human being who holds the keys to nobody's profit or loss, reward or punishment, and who has no credibility of his own. It comes from the merciful Lord whose Word admits of no error, and whose promise and whose warning are alike free of any apprehension of weakness or excuse.

**2. Cure — *shifāʾ li-mā fī al-ṣudūr*.** *Shifāʾ* means the removal of disease. *Ṣudūr* is the plural of *ṣadr*, the chest, and here it signifies the heart. So the Qur'an is a successful remedy for the diseases of the heart; it corrects and cures the heart the way a legendary elixir would. Ibn Kathir names the diseases it treats: "a cure from suspicion and doubts" — the Qur'an removes all the filth and shirk (the associating of partners with Allah) from hearts.

Here the scholars genuinely differ, and Maʿārif reports both sides. **Hasan al-Baṣrī** held that this attribute teaches us the Qur'an is a cure for the diseases of the heart *specifically*, and not for physical diseases (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī). **Other scholars** held that it is a cure for every disease, spiritual or physical; on their reading, spiritual diseases are simply far more harmful to a person than physical ones, and their treatment is not in everyone's control, so it is *those* that are named here — which does not entail that the Qur'an is no cure for bodily illness.

In support of the second view, Maʿārif cites two reports. Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that someone came to the Prophet ﷺ complaining that he felt he had a chest problem, and he ﷺ told him: recite the Qur'an, for Allah says *shifāʾ li-mā fī al-ṣudūr* — the Qur'an is a cure for such diseases as are found inside chests (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, from Ibn Marduwayh). Similarly, in a report from Sayyidnā Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ (may Allah be pleased with him), someone came saying he had a throat problem and was told the same thing: recite the Qur'an. Scholars of the Muslim community have gathered the properties and benefits of Qur'anic verses into whole books, drawn partly from ḥadīth narratives and the sayings of the Ṣaḥābah and partly from their own experiments and experience. Imām al-Ghazālī's work on Qur'anic properties is the best known in this area, and Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī's *Aʿmāl-i-Qurʼānī*, an abridgement of it, has been popular among Urdu readers for over fifty years.

But Maʿārif immediately guards the point from being cheapened. The real purpose of the Qur'an's revelation is to remove the diseases of the heart and soul; healing of the body follows only as a corollary. Those who recite it *only* to treat physical illness or to get worldly needs met — never bothering to correct their spiritual diseases, never heeding the instructions the Book actually gives — are described bluntly as low in sense and high in waywardness. Maʿārif quotes Iqbal's reproach that all such a person gains from Sūrah Yā Sīn is that reciting it makes death easier; had he pondered its meaning and message, its realities and insights, he would have gained far more of its benefits and blessings.

One further insight Maʿārif records from research-oriented commentators: the first attribute, *mawʿizah*, corresponds to a person's obvious, outward, physically accomplished deeds — what is known as the Sharīʿah, and the Qur'an is the best source for correcting and bettering them; while the second attribute, *shifāʾ li-mā fī al-ṣudūr*, corresponds to the hidden, inward, heart-oriented deeds, which these commentators call Ṭarīqah and Taṣawwuf — the names given here to that inner, heart-facing side of a person's life, as against the outward deeds named by Sharīʿah. Outside and inside, both are treated by the same Book.

**3. Guidance — *hudā*.** The word means guidance, the showing of the way, the leading onto it. The Qur'an invites human beings to the way of truth and faith. It invites them to ponder the great signs Allah has placed in the near and far ranges of the world — and even inside their own persons — and through them to recognise the Creator and Master of everything.

**4. Mercy — *raḥmah lil-muʼminīn*.** Read the ayah's ending carefully: the address opened to *all* humanity, but guidance and mercy are stated **for the believers**. Ibn Kathir draws that line out: the guidance and mercy of Allah are attained through the Qur'an, but this is only for those who believe in it and have firm faith in what it contains. He supports it with two other ayat — *"And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a cure and a mercy to those who believe, and it increases the wrongdoers nothing but loss"* (17:82), and *"Say: It is for those who believe, a guide and a cure"* (41:44). The same Book meets two different hearts and produces two different results.

## Ayah 58: the only joy worth the name

**"Say: In the bounty of Allah, and in His mercy — therein let them rejoice. That is better than what they amass."** Ibn Kathir reads it as a summons: rejoice in what has come from Allah, rejoice in the guidance and the religion of truth, for it is better than anything else they might rejoice in — better than the ruins of this world and its vanishing bloom.

**What are "bounty" and "mercy" here?** Maʿārif reports a ḥadīth from Sayyidnā Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: *faḍl*, the grace of Allah, denotes the Qur'an, and *raḥmah*, mercy, means that you were blessed with the *tawfīq* — the granted ability — to recite the Qur'an and to act in accordance with it (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, from Ibn Marduwayh). The same has been reported from Sayyidnā Barāʼ ibn ʿĀzib and Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with them). Many commentators say *faḍl* is the Qur'an and *raḥmah* is Islam — which comes to the same thing, since Islam in reality *is* Allah teaching us the Qur'an and granting us the ability to follow it in practice. And Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) narrates that *faḍl* is the Qur'an and *raḥmah* is the Prophet ﷺ himself — an interpretation that finds support in the ayah *"And We have not sent you except as a mercy for the worlds"* (21:107). Even this comes out at the same place, because acting on the Qur'an, which is Islam, ultimately reverts to following the lead the Prophet ﷺ gave through his word and deed.

So the thing a believer is commanded to be glad about is not an outcome, a possession or a status: it is the Book, and the fact of having been enabled to live by it.

**A grammatical detail worth noticing.** In the well-known recitation, *fal-yafraḥū* ("let **them** rejoice") is in the third person, even though the real addressees were those present there or living at that time — the exigency of the situation called for the second person, and indeed some recitations have it that way. Maʿārif, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, explains the wisdom in the third-person form: the mercy in question — the Prophet ﷺ, or Islam — was never restricted to those present or alive at that moment. It included even the generations that will be born right through the Day of Qiyāmah, the Day of Resurrection. The grammar quietly widens the circle to include you, reading this now.

**"Do not exult" and "let them rejoice" — is there a tension?** Maʿārif raises the objection directly. Another ayah says *"Do not exult; indeed Allah does not like the exultant"* (28:76) — where "do not exult" means rejoicing in triumph or intoxication — while here rejoicing is commanded in the imperative. Two answers are given. First, the rejoicing that is forbidden is over the fleeting enjoyments of a mortal world, while the rejoicing that is commanded is over the grace and mercy of Allah — different objects, different rulings. Second, what is prohibited is not rejoicing in the absolute sense but becoming euphoric and intoxicated in exultation, whereas what is permitted here is rejoicing in the absolute sense.

**"Better than what they amass."** Maʿārif explains why short-lived worldly wealth, possessions, comfort and recognition are simply not worth being happy about in any real sense. To begin with, however much a person has, it turns out to be not as much as he would have wished — it becomes a cycle that never ends. And there is the ever-lurking danger that it may start declining at any time. The grace and mercy of Allah are far better than the layers upon layers of wealth, property, recognition and power a person accumulates as the sum total of an entire life.

## Ayat 59–60: who has the right to say "forbidden"?

Now the passage turns, and the turn is sharp. Ayah 59 is a summons to produce evidence: *"Tell me, what provision Allah has sent down to you — and you have made of it lawful and unlawful. Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent a lie against Allah?"* Note the logic. The provision is His; He sent it down. So a ruling upon it has only two possible sources — divine permission, or forgery. There is no third option, and the questioner does not offer one.

**The occasion.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and others that this ayah was revealed to criticise the idolaters for what they used to make lawful and unlawful — categories like the *Baḥīrah*, the *Sāʼibah* and the *Waṣīlah*: livestock they marked out and then forbade to themselves by their own decree. He connects it to *"And they assign to Allah a share of the tilth and cattle which He has created"* (6:136).

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a narration recorded by Imām Aḥmad from Mālik ibn Naḍlah, who said: I came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ while in filthy clothes. He asked, "Do you have wealth?" I said yes. He asked, "What kind of wealth?" I said: all kinds — camels, slaves, horses, sheep. He said, **"If Allah gives you wealth, then let it be seen on you."** Then he ﷺ asked: is it not that your camels are born with healthy ears, and you take a knife and cut them and say "this is a *Baḥr*", and tear their skin and say "this is a *Ṣarm*", and prohibit them for yourself and your family? I replied yes. He said: **"What Allah has given you is lawful. Allah's Forearm is stronger than your forearm, and Allah's knife is sharper than your knife."** Ibn Kathir notes that the chain for this ḥadīth is a strong, good chain.

A man takes a blade to an animal's ear to enact a ruling he invented, and is reminded that the real blade and the real strength are not his.

**Why this is so serious.** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah criticised those who make lawful what He made unlawful, and unlawful what He made lawful, because such rulings rest on nothing but mere desires and false opinions unsupported by evidence or proof. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle flatly: whether a thing is ḥalāl (lawful) or ḥarām (unlawful) does not depend on human opinion. It is the special right and prerogative of Allah and His Messenger. Without an injunction from them, it is not permissible to call anything either ḥalāl or ḥarām.

**The warning in ayah 60.** *"And what do those who invent a lie against Allah think — on the Day of Resurrection?"* Ibn Kathir glosses it: what do they think will happen to them when they return to Us on that Day? Maʿārif notes that no lesser warning than the punishment of the Day of Qiyāmah has been attached to this crime.

**"Truly Allah is full of bounty to mankind, but most of them are ungrateful."** On the first half, two readings are given. **Ibn Jarīr** held that the bounty here lies in Allah postponing their punishment in this world — they forge lies against Him and are still given time. **Ibn Kathir** offers his own: the meaning could be that the grace for people lies in the good benefits Allah has made permissible for them in this world or in their religion; and He has not prohibited them anything except what is harmful to them in their world and the Hereafter. On that reading, ayah 60 speaks to the very question the passage has been raising — the One who legislates is the One whose permissions are benefits and whose prohibitions fall only on what harms.

And then the sting of the ending. Ibn Kathir explains "most of them are ungrateful" precisely: **so they prohibited what Allah had bestowed upon them, and made it hard and narrow upon themselves.** They made some things lawful and others unlawful. The idolaters committed these actions when they set laws for themselves — and so did the People of the Book, when they invented innovations in their religion. Ingratitude here is not merely failing to say thank you; it is taking a gift and turning it into a restriction, refusing the very ease that was handed to you.

## Living it

**Take the medicine as medicine.** The Qur'an is named a cure for what is in the chests. Ibn Kathir specifies the ailments — suspicion, doubt, the filth of shirk. If your relationship with the Book never touches those, you are holding an elixir and using it as decoration.

**Relocate your joy.** Ayah 58 does not merely permit rejoicing; it commands it, and names its proper object: the Qur'an, and the ability to live by it. Maʿārif's argument is worth keeping close whenever accumulation starts to look like happiness — no amount ever turns out to be the amount you wanted, and whatever you have gathered may start declining at any time.

**Guard your tongue on ḥalāl and ḥarām.** Ayah 59 does not only rebuke pagan Arabia. Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān put it as a standing principle: whenever anyone declares something forbidden or permitted without authority from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, they are answering a question Allah never gave them the right to answer — and ayah 60 tells them when that answer will be reviewed.

**Do not narrow what Allah has widened.** The closing phrase of ayah 60 names self-imposed hardship as a form of ingratitude. The Prophet ﷺ told Mālik ibn Naḍlah that what Allah had given him was lawful, and that when Allah gives wealth its effect should be seen on the one given. Receiving Allah's provision gratefully, and using it as He permitted, is itself part of what this passage asks.

passages.title: Nothing escapes Him; the friends of Allah
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that nothing he is engaged in — no task, no portion of Qur'an recited, no deed of his community — takes place outside Allah's witnessing (ayah 61); then He announces who His close friends are and what awaits them (ayat 62–64). What binds the two halves is a single divine gaze seen from two sides: to the one who forgets it, an inescapable audit; to the believer, the safest place in the world to stand. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link explicit — describing Allah's all-encompassing knowledge here appears aimed at consoling the Prophet ﷺ, that his enemies cannot harm him in any way, for he was under Allah's protection. Ayat 62–64 widen that protection to every believer who lives in awareness of Allah.

## Ayah 61 — nothing slips through

**Watch who is being addressed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the verse this way: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and he is being told that nothing he does — by way of his work or his recitation of the Qur'an — remains hidden from Allah. And the same is said of everyone else: whatever all human beings do stands before Him. Not a single particle in the heavens or the earth is concealed from Him; everything is written in the clear Book, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies as *al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*, the Preserved Tablet.

Ibn Kathir glosses the closing phrase — *but We are Witness thereof when you are doing it* — as: *We are watching and hearing you when you engage in that thing.*

**Ibn Kathir's argument from the small to the great.** Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ, says Ibn Kathir, that He knows and is well acquainted with all the affairs and conditions of him, of his Ummah, and of all creation at all times — during every hour and second. He then builds a ladder of evidence from the Qur'an itself:

- *And with Him are the keys of the Ghayb, none knows them but He… not a leaf falls, but He knows it. There is not a grain in the darkness of the earth nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record* (6:59) — so, says Ibn Kathir, He is Well-Aware of the movement of the trees and other inanimate objects.
- *There is not a moving creature on earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but are communities like you* (6:38), and *no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah* (11:6) — so He is Well-Aware of all grazing beasts and their sustenance.
- The conclusion: if this is His knowledge of the movement of these things, then what about His knowledge of the movement of the creatures commanded to worship Him? Hence: *And put your trust in the Almighty, the Most Merciful, Who sees you when you stand up, and your movements among those who fall prostrate* (26:217–219).

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir attaches to this verse the Prophet's ﷺ own answer when Jibrīl asked him about *iḥsān* (excellence in worship): *It is that you worship Allah as if you are seeing Him. But since you do not see Him, be certain that He is watching you.* The verse states the fact — He is witnessing you; *iḥsān* is what a believer does with that fact.

## Ayah 62 — the announcement

Ibn Kathir renders the verse: *Behold! The Awliyāʼ (friends and allies) of Allah, no fear shall come upon them nor shall they grieve.*

**What *walī* actually means.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word carefully. *Awliyāʼ* is the plural of *walī*, used in Arabic in a double sense: "near," and also "friend" or someone held "dear." There is a common degree of nearness and love between Allah and everything He has made — no living thing is exempt from it, and without it nothing in this universe would have come into being. There is a further degree of friendship, love and nearness specific to particular servants of Allah — what the commentary calls **nearness in love** — and those blessed with it are the *Awliyāʼ* of Allah.

It quotes a *ḥadīth qudsī* (a report in which the Prophet ﷺ conveys words from Allah) in which Allah says that His servant keeps earning His nearness through voluntary acts of worship (*nafl ʿibādāt*) until He too turns to him in love; and when He loves him, He becomes his ear, his eye, his hands and feet — so that whatever he hears, sees and does, he does through Him. The commentary's own summary keeps this within proper bounds: in short, it means that virtually nothing issues forth from such a person against the pleasure of his Lord. Not a man becoming divine.

The degrees of this *wilāyah* — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses as the station of nearness or friendship with Allah — are endless. Its highest degree belongs to the prophets, since every prophet must of necessity be a *walī* of Allah, and within that, the highest station belongs to the foremost among the prophets, Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ.

## Ayah 63 — the Qur'an defines its own term

The Qur'an does not leave "friend of Allah" as an open title for anyone to claim: ayah 63 defines it on the spot — *those who believed, and have taqwā*. Ibn Kathir states it flatly: His *Awliyāʼ* are those who believe and have *taqwā* of Allah, as He Himself defined them; **every pious person who fears Allah is a friend of Allah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same phrase as those who believed and *remained* pious, righteous and fearful of Allah.

**The two visible marks.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the practical signature of this station: abundance of *dhikr* and constancy in obedience — to remember Allah always, under all conditions and circumstances. When these two attributes are present in a person, he is called a *walī* of Allah; whoever lacks either one is not included in that category. And whoever has both — there is no limit to his ranks, lower and higher.

**A warning worth its weight.** Tafsīr Mazharī, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, notes a prevailing assumption among people that knowing what is hidden (*kashf*), performing extraordinary feats (*karāmah*), or claiming awareness of the Unseen are the signs of someone being among the friends of Allah. This is nothing but error and self-deception. There are thousands of *Awliyāʼ* not credited with anything of the sort that could be termed authentically proved — while, in sharp contrast, reports of hidden and unseen things are accredited to people whose very basic *īmān* is not correct.

**The real sign.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points instead to a *ḥadīth qudsī* referred to in Tafsīr Mazharī, in which Allah says: *From among My servants, My Awliyāʼ are those who are remembered when I am remembered, and when they are remembered I am remembered.* And in a narration from Sayyidah Asmāʼ bint Yazīd reported in Ibn Mājah, the Prophet ﷺ gave their identity as *those who, when one sees them, remind one of Allah*. The test is simple: if by sitting in someone's company you are given the *tawfīq* — the granted ability — of remembering Allah, and relief from worldly concerns, that is a sign of his being a *walī* of Allah.

**Loved for nothing but Allah.** Ibn Kathir cites a report recorded by Ibn Jarīr from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *Among the servants of Allah there will be those whom the Prophets and the martyrs will consider fortunate.* It was said, "Who are these, O Messenger of Allah, so we may love them?" He said: *These are people who loved one another for the sake of Allah without any other interest like money or kinship. Their faces will be light, upon platforms of light. They shall have no fear when fear shall come upon people. Nor shall they grieve when others grieve* — and then he recited this very verse.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries a separate and much shorter narration, also going back to Abū Hurayrah, by a different route — Tafsīr Mazharī, quoting Ibn Marduwayh. In it the Prophet ﷺ was asked who the people meant by *Awliyāʼ Allāh* in this verse were, and he answered: *those who love each other only for Allah — without having any worldly interest in between.*

## "No fear, no grief" — what is actually being promised

Ibn Kathir is precise about the two halves: **no fear** — from the future horrors they will face in the Hereafter; **nor shall they grieve** — over anything left behind in this world.

But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to let the promise be read carelessly. If it means only their deliverance from fear and grief once they are admitted to Paradise, the verse registers no peculiarity of the *Awliyāʼ* — all the people of Paradise, delivered from the Fire, will be enjoying that very state. Many commentators therefore say the freedom covers the present world and the Hereafter both: what is unique about the friends of Allah is that they remain protected from fear and grief **even in the present world**.

Then the harder objection: observation bears out that — not to mention the friends of Allah — even the Prophets, peace be upon them, are not secure from fear and grief in this mortal world; in fact their fear of Allah and humbleness before Him is far more pronounced than others'. *Among Our servants only those who have knowledge (really) fear Allah* (35:28). *And those who are fearful of the punishment of their Lord — indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not to be un-feared* (70:27).
