It appears in a hadith of *Shamāʼil al-Tirmidhī* that the Prophet ﷺ would more often than not look concerned and pensive, and he himself said, *I fear Allah more than all of you.* And there are countless events relating to Sayyidnā Abū Bakr, Sayyidnā ʿUmar and the rest of the Companions and the Tābiʿīn, which tell us how intensely they grieved and how genuinely they feared what would happen to them in the Hereafter.

**ʿAllāmah Ālūsī's resolution**, quoted from *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*: that the friends of Allah are protected against fear and grief in this world has to be seen in terms of what usually happens here. Worldly people are chronically attached to their mundane agenda — convenience, comfort, wealth and recognition; the slightest shortfall in any of these makes them nervous, as if they were going to die without it. The station of the friends of Allah is far higher: in their sight these transitory things are not worth going about acquiring. So overshadowed are they with the fear of Allah and their humbleness before Him that they have no use for worldly sorrow and comfort, or profit and loss.

So the promise is not numbness, and certainly not freedom from the fear of Allah — that fear is the mark of the friends. What is lifted is anxiety over the world's small losses.

## Ayah 64 — the good news, delivered twice

*For them is good news, in the life of the present world, and in the Hereafter.* Ibn Kathir narrates from Ibn Jarīr that ʿUbādah bin al-Ṣāmit recited this verse to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "We know the good news of the Hereafter, it is Paradise. But what is the good news in this world?" He said: *It is the good dream that a servant may see or it is seen about him. This dream is one part from forty-four or seventy parts of Prophethood.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same identification of the worldly good news through an entirely separate narration — reported, it says, by al-Bukhārī from Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah: the Prophet ﷺ said they are the true dreams one sees oneself, or that are seen by someone else with him in them, in which there is good news for them.

Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr that the Prophet ﷺ, after reciting this verse, said: *The good dream that comes as good news for the believer is a part of forty-nine parts of prophethood. So if anyone of you has a good dream, he should narrate it to others. But if he has a dream that he dislikes, then it is from Shayṭān to make him sad. He should blow to his left three times, and say "Allāhu Akbar," and should not mention it to anyone.*

**A second, in this world.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Abū Dharr asked, "O Messenger of Allah! What about a man who does deeds that the people commend him for?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *That is the good news that has been expedited for the believer.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites that same saying — attributing it to Muslim and al-Baghawī — for another form of worldly good news: that Muslims at large come to love someone and take him to be good without any personal motive or interest; being taken as good and praiseworthy is, as it puts it, good news in ready cash. Not permission to chase praise; reassurance that sincere love from believers is a sign, not a payment.

**And a third: the reception at death.** Ibn Kathir mentions the further view — "it was also said" — that the good news is the glad tidings the angels bring the believer at the time of death, of Paradise and forgiveness, as in *those who say "Our Lord is Allah" and then they stand straight and firm, on them the angels will descend: "Fear not, nor grieve! But receive the glad tidings of Paradise which you have been promised! We have been your friends in the life of this world and are so in the Hereafter…"* (41:30–32) — the angels say *fear not, nor grieve*, and call themselves *awliyāʼ* of the believers. In the hadith narrated by al-Barāʼ, the Prophet ﷺ said that when death approaches the believer, angels with white faces and white clothes come to him and say, *O good soul! Come out to comfort and provision and a Lord who is not angry.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report from al-Ṭabarānī, from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿUmar, that people who recite *lā ilāha illā Allāh* will experience no fright at the time of death, nor inside the grave, nor at the time they rise from it — shaking the dust off as they rise, saying: *Praised is Allah who has removed from us all grief* (35:34).

**In the Hereafter**, Ibn Kathir cites: *The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will meet them: "This is your Day which you were promised"* (21:103); and the believing men and women whose light runs forward before them, greeted with *Glad tidings for you this Day! Gardens under which rivers flow* (57:12).

**"No change can there be in the Words of Allah."** Ibn Kathir's comment: this promise does not change or breach or fall short; it is decreed and firm, and going to happen undoubtedly. Ayah 61 closed off every escape from Allah's knowledge; ayah 64 closes off every escape from His promise. *This is indeed the supreme success* — the verse names it, so we need not.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh Pānīpatī in *Tafsīr Mazharī*, is concrete about the road to this station. Individuals of this Ummah could acquire this degree of *wilāyah* only through the company of the Prophet ﷺ; it is from there that the profound relationship with Allah which was part of his blessed persona is partly passed on to the friends of Allah in this Ummah, each according to his ambition and capacity. That benefit of companionship was available to the Companions with no one in between — which is why the degree of their *wilāyah* was higher than that of all later *Awliyāʼ*. Later people derive the benefit through one or more intermediaries, and the more the intermediaries, the more pronounced the difference becomes. Only those coloured with the word, deed and message of the Prophet ﷺ, following his Sunnah in love and obedience, can serve as such an intermediary. The blueprint has three parts:

1. **Being in the company of a *walī* of Allah** — with a hard condition attached: to be beneficial, that company has to be of those who are themselves friends of Allah and staunch followers of the Sunnah. Those who do not observe and follow the Sunnah are themselves deprived of this degree, no matter how many wonders (*kashf* and *karāmāt*) issue forth from them; whereas someone who has the stated attributes is a *walī* of Allah even if nothing of the sort ever issued forth from him.
2. **Remaining obedient to his good counsel.**
3. **Remembering Allah abundantly** (*dhikrullāh*) — on the *masnūn* pattern, the method established in the Sunnah. Dhikr, when frequent and sincere, adds to the lustre of the mirror of the heart until it becomes worthy of receiving reflections from the light of *wilāyah*. It appears in hadith that everything has a method of furbishing it, and what furbishes the heart is *dhikrullāh* — the same reported by al-Bayhaqī from a narration of Sayyidnā Ibn ʿUmar.

Two supports are added. Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd related that a person asked the Prophet ﷺ about someone who loves a spiritually noble person but is unable to reach his level in deeds; he ﷺ said, *everyone shall be with the one he loves* — which tells us that love and company of the friends of Allah is itself a means of acquiring nearness to Allah. And al-Bayhaqī, in *Shuʿab al-Īmān*, reports that the Prophet ﷺ told Sayyidnā Razīn of a principle of faith by which one may attain success in this world and the Hereafter: take to the company of *ahl adh-dhikr* — the people who remember Allah — as indispensable; when you are alone, move your tongue with the remembrance of Allah as much as you can; whomever you love, love for Allah, and whomever you hate, hate for Allah.

**Back to where the passage began.** Ayah 61 says He is watching and hearing you in whatever you are engaged in; ayah 64 says His friends have good news here and hereafter, and His word will not change. Between them lies the whole invitation: live as though seen — because you are — and the gaze that would otherwise frighten you becomes the very reason you are unafraid.

passages.title: Do not grieve: all honour belongs to Allah
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These three ayat are one act of consolation. In ayah 65 Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ not to let the talk of his opponents grieve him, and gives the reason in a single sentence: all power and honour belong to Allah, who hears and knows. Ibn Kathīr then follows the passage's own order: Allah "stated that to Him is the dominion of the heavens and earth" (ayah 66), and then "informed us that He is the One Who made the night for His servants to rest therein" (ayah 67). Ownership first, then the sky itself. The thread running through all three is where power actually sits — and therefore whose opinion is worth grieving over.

## A brief word on the ayah just before

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its comment here by looking back at ayah 64, which promised the friends of Allah good news — *basharah* — in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. The good news of the Hereafter, it explains, comes at the time of death, when the spirit is taken to Allah and he hears that Paradise is his, and again on the Day of Qiyāmah, when he rises from the grave and is welcomed to Paradise; it cites here a report of al-Ṭabarānī from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said people who say *lā ilāha illa'llāh* — there is no god but Allah — will feel no fright at death, nor in the grave, nor when they rise from it, rising instead with the words *al-ḥamdu lillāhi'lladhī adhhaba ʿannā'l-ḥazan*, "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us all grief" (35:34). As for good news in this world, it names the true dream a believer sees, or that someone else sees with him in it (reported by al-Bukhārī from Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him), and that Muslims at large come to love someone and take him to be good with no personal motive or interest behind it — of which the Prophet ﷺ said that being taken as good and praiseworthy is, for a true Muslim, good news in ready cash (Muslim and al-Baghawī).

That is the ground our passage stands on rather than the passage itself. One small thing is worth carrying across, offered as a reader's observation and not as something the commentators say: the word for the grief removed in 35:34, *al-ḥazan*, shares its root with the verb in our ayah, *lā yaḥzunka* — "let it not grieve you."

## "Do not let their words grieve you" (ayah 65)

Ibn Kathīr is direct about who is meant. Allah said to His Messenger ﷺ: do not grieve **"because of the remarks of these idolators."** This is not abstract advice about criticism in general; it is about the actual things being said about him by the idolaters around him.

Notice what the command does *not* say. It does not say they will stop, and it does not say answer them. It addresses the grief itself. And Ibn Kathīr reads the ayah as carrying its own remedy: **"depend on Allah and ask for His help. Put your trust in Him."** The alternative to being crushed by what people say is not a thicker skin — it is leaning your whole weight on the One who actually holds things.

There is also a mercy in the phrasing. The Arabic does not say simply "do not grieve"; the words themselves are made the subject — *wa-lā yaḥzunka qawluhum*, "let their speech not grieve you." The grief is treated as something their words are trying to do *to* him. He is not being scolded for a feeling. He is being told to refuse an assault.

## "Surely all power and honour belong to Allah — all of it" (ayah 65)

*al-ʿIzzah* is the word being translated, and English has to reach for two words at once to carry it. Ibn Kathīr's rendering does exactly that: **"For all power and honor belong to Allah."** Both senses matter here, because both are what is at stake whenever someone is being belittled.

And the ayah adds *jamīʿan*: all of it, entire, without remainder. If even a fraction of real honour were distributed among those doing the mocking, their contempt would carry weight. Since none of it is, their words are noise made by people who own nothing.

Ibn Kathīr then adds something striking: **"All might and honor belong to Him, His Messenger and the believers."** This does not contradict *jamīʿan*; it follows from it. Honour is not a substance the believer possesses independently — it is Allah's, and it reaches His Messenger ﷺ and the believers through Him. Which means a believer who is despised by everyone around him may still be the honoured one in the room.

## "He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower" (ayah 65)

The two names are fitted precisely to a grievance about *speech*. Ibn Kathīr glosses them: **"He hears the utterances of His servants and knows their affairs."**

They said it — He heard it. They meant something by it, and had motives behind it they never spoke aloud — He knows that too. Nothing said against the Prophet ﷺ went unheard, and nothing hidden behind it was hidden from Allah. That is at once a comfort to the one being insulted and a caution to the one insulting.

## Everything belongs to Him — so what exactly are they worshipping? (ayah 66)

Ayah 66 opens with an attention-particle rendered in Ibn Kathīr's text as **"Behold!"** — a call to look up before the point lands: to Allah belongs *whosoever* is in the heavens and *whosoever* is in the earth.

Ibn Kathīr's summary of the argument is compact. Allah **"stated that to Him is the dominion of the heavens and earth. But the idolators worship idols, that own nothing and can neither harm nor benefit anyone."**

Follow the logic. If every being in the heavens and the earth already belongs to Allah, then anything a person sets up alongside Him is itself owned — and Ibn Kathīr's words are blunt about what such an object can do: nothing, neither harm nor benefit. So worship directed to it is not a competing loyalty. It is an act aimed at something that owns nothing and can do nothing.

The ayah then diagnoses why people do it anyway. **"They have no evidence to base their worship on them. They only follow their own conjecture, lies, and ultimately — falsehood."** Conjecture — guesswork, supposition — is what is named: not proof, not evidence, not a sound argument. And this quietly demolishes the basis on which the mockers of ayah 65 were speaking. Their scorn was not the verdict of people who knew something. It was the confidence of people guessing.

## Night and day: the argument you sleep through (ayah 67)

Having settled the matter cosmically, the passage comes very close to home. Ayah 67 does not point at thunder or mountains. It points at your last twenty-four hours.

**The night.** Ibn Kathīr: Allah **"is the One Who made the night for His servants to rest therein from weariness and exhaustion."** The ayah says *li-taskunū fīh* — that you may come to rest in it, settle, be still. Darkness is not merely an absence that happens to fall; it is provision, arranged for bodies that wear out.

**The day.** Of the daytime the ayah says *wa'n-nahāra mubṣiran*, which Ibn Kathīr's text renders **"And the day to make things visible (to you)"**, and explains: **"bright and clear for them to seek livelihood and to travel to fulfill their needs."** The day is described by what it does for the eye — it is the stretch in which earning and travelling become possible.

Between them, the two describe the whole of an ordinary life: exhaustion and recovery, work and stillness. And the ayah insists on the author of the arrangement — *He it is Who has appointed for you* the night and the day. The One who arranges that is the One telling His Messenger ﷺ not to be grieved by a handful of remarks.

**"Verily, in this are Ayat for a people who listen."** Ibn Kathīr: **"Those who hear these proofs and take a lesson from them. These Ayat can lead them to realize the greatness of their Creator and Sustainer."**

So the test is not eyesight. Everyone sees night fall and morning break. Hearing here, on Ibn Kathīr's reading, means hearing that changes you — receiving the proof and taking the lesson from it, so that it leads somewhere: to realising the greatness of the Creator and Sustainer. (A reader may also notice that in ayah 65 Allah is *al-Samīʿ*, the One who hears, while in ayah 67 people are sorted by whether *they* hear — a resonance in the Arabic, though not a point the commentators make.)

## Living it

- **Take the command literally.** When words about you hurt, the instruction is not to pretend they do not, but to refuse to let them settle in — and Ibn Kathīr tells us how: depend on Allah, ask Him for His help, put your trust in Him. Grief handed over is grief in the right hands.
- **Check where you keep your honour.** If your sense of worth is stored in other people's estimation, every remark can rob you. Ayah 65 says the whole of *al-ʿizzah* is Allah's, and Ibn Kathīr adds that it belongs to Him, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. Nearness to Allah is the only account that gossip cannot drain.
- **Remember that He heard it.** You do not have to assemble the case for your own vindication. He hears the utterances of His servants and knows their affairs — every word, and every affair behind it.
- **Test your certainties.** Ayah 66 condemns not only the idols but the reasoning: worship with no evidence to base it on, following only conjecture. Ask of your own convictions, and of other people's confident opinions about you: what is the evidence, or is this only guesswork?
- **Let the night and the day preach.** Resting when tired and working when the light comes are acts of being cared for. Ayah 67 asks you to be among those who hear these proofs and take the lesson from them — noticing, at least once a day, whose arrangement it is.

passages.title: Refuting the claim that Allah has a son
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move as one breath: a false claim about Allah is quoted (68) and answered on the spot with three separate arguments; then the people who make such claims are told the verdict on them (69); then the objection that they seem to be doing perfectly well is met head-on (70). Ibn Kathir treats the three together and heads the whole section, **"Allah is Far Above taking a Wife or having Children."**

## The claim, and the first word of the answer

Ayah 68 opens by quoting them: *"Allah has offspring"* — or, as the wording in Ibn Kathir's text has it, *"Allah has begotten a son."* Ibn Kathir opens his comment by naming exactly what is happening: **"Allah criticizes those who claim that He has… begotten a son."**

The answer begins before any argument is made. **Subḥānahu** — *"Glory be to Him."* This word is a declaration that Allah is far removed above what has just been said, and Ibn Kathir glosses it exactly so: **"He is Greater than that and above it."** Notice what the order teaches. The claim is not first weighed and then rejected; it is first *repudiated*, and only afterwards taken apart. Some statements about Allah are answered first with reverence and second with reasoning. And notice the direction of Ibn Kathir's words — the claim is not merely untrue, it is beneath Him. It is not something Allah lacks. It is something He is above.

## "He is al-Ghaniyy" — the argument from need

The first argument is a single statement about who Allah is. **Al-Ghaniyy** — Ibn Kathir renders it *"Rich (free of all needs)"* and explains: **"He is Self-Sufficient, free of want or need of anything. Everything else is in desperate need of Him."**

Feel how that dismantles the claim. Why does anyone want a child? For an heir, for help, for continuation, for the part of yourself that outlasts you — every one of those is a need being answered. To say Allah took a child is to say there was a gap in Him that a child fills. But al-Ghaniyy means the gap does not exist. And Ibn Kathir makes the sentence run both ways: not only does Allah need nothing, *everything else* is in desperate need of Him. Need is entirely on one side of the line. A being with no need does not acquire a son.

## "His is all that is in the heavens and the earth" — the argument from ownership

The second argument is one clause: *"His is all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth."* Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion in the form of a question you are meant to feel the force of: **"So how can He have a son from what He has created? Everything and everyone belongs to Him and is His servant."**

The point is about categories. Ibn Kathir's sentence leaves only two: Allah, and what He has created. And everything on the created side is described in the same two words — *belongs to Him*, and *is His servant*. Every angel, every prophet, every soul in the heavens and on the earth falls there. Anyone you might nominate as His child is already something He made and owns, and already stands to Him as a servant. There is no one left over to be a son.

## "You have no warrant for this" — the argument from evidence

The third argument turns on them: *"No warrant have you for this."* Ibn Kathir explains the word plainly: **"you have no proof for the lies and falsehood that you claim."**

This is precise. A claim about what Allah is and is not could only be known if Allah made it known. So the demand is fair: produce your proof. There is none.

Then the closing question: *"Do you say against Allah what you know not?"* Ibn Kathir does not read this as a mild rhetorical flourish. He says: **"This is a severe threat and a firm warning."** The sin being named is not only that the statement is false, but that it was said about Allah without knowledge.

## What the heavens make of it

Ibn Kathir then writes, **"Similarly, Allah threatened and said,"** and sets beside our ayah Allah's words in Sūrah Maryam (19:88–95): *"And they say: 'The Most Gracious has begotten a son.' Indeed you have brought forth a terribly evil thing. Whereby the heavens are almost torn, and the earth is split asunder, and the mountains fall in ruins, that they ascribe a son to the Most Gracious."*

Read that slowly. The claim is made in a moment, in an ordinary human voice, and the physical universe nearly comes apart under it. And the passage keeps going along the very lines our ayah drew: *"But it is not suitable for the Most Gracious that He should beget a son. There is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto the Most Gracious as a servant. Verily, He knows each one of them, and has counted them a full counting. And everyone of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection."*

There is the ownership argument again — *all of them come as servants* — and then something further: each one arrives on the Day of Resurrection **alone**. Counted, known, and singular. No lineage, no family standing, no relation to Allah but servanthood. The very category the claim tried to invent is the one category that will not exist on that Day.

## Ayah 69: the verdict, announced out loud

Ayah 69 begins with **"Say"** — the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to state the outcome publicly, not merely to know it: *"Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will not succeed."*

Ibn Kathir applies the words directly to the people of ayah 68: **"Then Allah warned the liars that fabricated the claim that He has begotten a son."** But notice that the wording of the ayah itself is general — *those who fabricate lies against Allah* — which is why the rebuke of the previous ayah, *"Do you say against Allah what you know not,"* lands on precisely the same target.

And Ibn Kathir closes off every corner of the verdict: **"He warned that they will not succeed, never prospering in this world or in the Hereafter."** Not a delayed success, not a partial one, not one arena spared. It is total.

## Ayah 70: "but they seem to be doing fine"

That verdict raises the obvious objection: these people are not visibly failing. They have wealth, standing, time. Ayah 70 answers before the objection can be voiced.

*"(A brief) enjoyment in this world!"* Ibn Kathir's gloss is a single phrase: **"meaning, only a short period."** The words stand almost dismissively on their own — *just an enjoyment, in this world.* That is the whole of it.

Ibn Kathir explains what is really happening inside that comfort: **"In this world Allah will lead them, step-by-step, to their ruin. He will give them respite and put up with them for a while. He will allow them to have little enjoyment,"** and he cites Allah's words *"then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment"* (31:24). The ease is not an exemption from the verdict. It is part of how the verdict arrives.

Then the ayah moves in steps: *"and then unto Us will be their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment because they used to disbelieve."* Ibn Kathir marks the return as being **"on the Day of Resurrection."** Enjoyment, return, torment: three stages, and only the first is visible from here.

And the ending gives the reason. Ibn Kathir: **"We shall make them taste the painful punishment because of their Kufr and lies about Allah"** — Kufr meaning their disbelief. The punishment is fastened to what they chose, and to what they said about Him.

## The contrast the sūrah is drawing

Read this passage against the one just before it. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, ayah 64 said that for the friends of Allah there is **good news in the worldly life and in the Hereafter.** Now set the two ledgers side by side.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the good news of the Hereafter comes at the time of death, when the dying believer hears that Paradise is his, and again on the Day of Qiyamah when he rises from his grave and is welcomed to it. It cites the report of al-Ṭabarānī from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said the people who say **lā ilāha illa'llāh** — there is no god but Allah — *"will not experience any fright at the time of death, nor inside the grave, nor at the time they rise from it,"* rising and shaking the dust off, saying, *"Praised is Allah who has removed from us all grief"* (35:34).

As for the good news in this world, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two forms of it. The first is the true dream: the Prophet ﷺ said they are *"the true dreams one sees himself or are seen by someone else with him in it and, in which, there is good news for them"* (reported by al-Bukhārī from Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah). The second is being genuinely loved and thought well of by the Muslims at large, with no personal motive or interest behind it — of which the Prophet ﷺ said that this is, for a true Muslim, *"good news in ready cash"* (Muslim and al-Baghawī).

Now set that beside ayah 70: a brief enjoyment, then the return, then the severest torment. The two columns are exact opposites — and what separates them is what a person says about Allah. One column says *there is no god but Allah*. The other says *Allah has taken a child*.

## Living it

**Guard your tongue about Allah.** The heart of the rebuke in ayah 68 is not merely that they were wrong; it is *"Do you say against Allah what you know not?"* — which Ibn Kathir calls a severe threat and a firm warning. That question reaches anyone who speaks about Allah, or about His religion and rulings, on the strength of feeling, habit or assumption rather than knowledge. The safest four words a believer owns are still "I do not know."

**Ask what proof you have.** *"No warrant have you for this"* — Ibn Kathir: *you have no proof.* That standard is worth turning inwards as well as outwards. For anything you hold about Allah, there should be an answer to the question: where did this come from?

**Do not read comfort as approval.** Ayah 70 corrects a very natural mistake — assuming that people whose worldly life is going well must be right, and that our own ease means we are safe. Ibn Kathir's description of respite as a step-by-step leading to ruin should permanently uncouple the two in our minds. The world's verdict on someone is not Allah's.

**Let *subḥānahu* be a reflex.** When something unworthy of Allah is said in front of you, this passage models the response before it models the argument: declare Him far above it, and only then explain why.

passages.title: Noah's stand and the messengers after him
passages.tafsir:
**These four ayat put the story of Nuh (Noah) in front of the Quraysh as a mirror.** Ayah 71 gives us his words — a lone man telling an entire hostile people that they may do their worst; ayah 72 strips away any suspicion of self-interest and names his religion; ayah 73 shows how it ended, with a rescue and a drowning; ayah 74 widens the lens to the messengers who came after him. What holds the unit together is a single question the passage keeps asking: **when a caller to Allah stands alone against a whole society, who is left standing at the end?**

## "Recite to them" — who is really being addressed

The passage opens with a command to the Prophet ﷺ: *And recite to them the news of Nuh.* Ibn Kathir is precise about the audience. "Recite to them" means **relate it to the disbelievers of the Quraysh who belied you and rejected you**; "the news of Nuh" means his story and news with his people who belied *him* — tell them how Allah destroyed them and caused every last one of them to drown. Then Ibn Kathir states the purpose plainly: *"Let this be a lesson for your people, lest they will be destroyed like them."*

So this is not history told for its own sake. It is history aimed. The story is being recited to a people who are, at that very moment, doing to their messenger what Nuh's people did to him.

## Ayah 71: the stand itself

Nuh's speech is short, and every clause of it is load-bearing.

**"If my stay among you and my reminding you of the signs of Allah is hard on you…"** The word rendered "my stay" is *maqāmī*, and Ibn Kathir unfolds the whole clause as: *if you find that it is too much of an offense that I should live among you and preach to you the revelation of Allah and His signs and proofs.* What they find unbearable is not one accusation but a whole grating presence: his continued residence among them, and his continual *tadhkīr* — his reminding them — of the āyāt of Allah, His signs and proofs. Nuh voices their grievance for them, in their own terms. He knows exactly how heavy he has become to his people.

**"…then upon Allah I have placed my trust."** Ibn Kathir completes the sense: *"then I do not care what you think, and I will not stop inviting you."* Notice the structure of the sentence. The condition is their hostility; the consequence is not defiance for its own sake but *tawakkul* — trust placed in Allah. He can afford not to care about their opinion because he has already handed the outcome to the One whose verdict decides everything. Reliance on Allah is what makes his refusal to stop something other than mere stubbornness.

**"So devise your plot, you and your partners."** Ibn Kathir: *"get together with all of your deities (idols and statues) that you call upon beside Allah."* This is the sharpest edge of the challenge. He is not merely daring the men; he is daring what they worship. Bring the whole coalition and see what it produces.

**"And let not your plot be in confusion for you."** Ibn Kathir explains: *"do not be confused about this, rather come and let us settle this together if you claim that you are truthful."* No murkiness, no half-measures, no hesitation — settle it openly.

**"And give me no respite."** Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is the most striking line in the whole comment: *"Do not give me respite even for one hour. Whatever you can do, go ahead and do it. I do not care, and I do not fear you, because you are not standing on anything."* That last clause carries the logic of the entire passage. Falsehood has nothing under it. A man who has grasped that can invite the worst his enemies have.

**A parallel Ibn Kathir draws.** He notes that this is similar to what Hud said to his people: *"I call Allah to witness, and you bear witness, that I am free from that which you ascribe as partners in worship with Him. So plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord!"* (11:54–55). The same three moves in the same order: disown their partners, invite their worst, declare reliance on Allah.

## Ayah 72: nothing to gain, and a name for his religion

**"But if you turn away…"** — Ibn Kathir: *if you belie the message and turn away from obedience.* **"…then no reward have I asked of you"** — *"I have not asked you anything for my advice."* His entire life's work among them has been unbilled. If they walk away he loses no fee. Their rejection costs him nothing, which means his persistence was never about them paying.

**"My reward is only from Allah."** The account is with Someone else, and it is safe.

**"And I have been commanded to be of the Muslims."** Ibn Kathir takes this half-sentence and builds his largest theme on it: **Islam is the religion of all of the Prophets, from the first to the last. Their laws and their rules may be of different types, but the religion is the same.** He supports this with a chain of verses:

- *"To each among you, We have prescribed a law and a clear way"* (5:48) — on which Ibn 'Abbas said: **"A way and a Sunnah."** So the difference between prophets is a difference of prescribed law and way.
- Ibrahim: *"Submit (be a Muslim)!" He said, "I have submitted myself to the Lord of all that exists"* — and he enjoined the same upon his sons, as did Ya'qub: *"then die not except as Muslims"* (2:131–132).
- Yusuf: *"Cause me to die as a Muslim, and join me with the righteous"* (12:101).
- Musa: *"O my people! If you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him if you are Muslims"* (10:84) — note that Musa, like Nuh here, joins reliance on Allah to submission.
- The magicians: *"Our Lord! pour out on us patience, and cause us to die as Muslims"* (7:126).
- Bilqis: *"My Lord! Verily, I have wronged myself, and I submit together with Sulayman to Allah, the Lord of all that exists"* (27:44).
- The Tawrah: *"Verily, We did send down the Tawrah, therein was guidance and light, by which the Prophets, judged for the Jews"* (5:44).
- Al-Hawariyyin, the disciples: *"We believe. And bear witness that we are Muslims"* (5:111).
- And the last of the Messengers and the leader of mankind ﷺ: *"Verily, my Salah, my sacrifice, my living, and my dying are for Allah, the Lord of all that exists. He has no partner. And of this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims"* (6:162–163) — on which Ibn Kathir clarifies: **meaning, from this Ummah.**

Ibn Kathir then cites what he describes as an authentic hadith, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"We, the Prophets are brothers with (the same father but) different mothers. Our religion is the same."* Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: *"we should worship Allah alone without partners while having different laws."* Brothers sharing one father, raised by different mothers — one worship, differing legislations.

Why does this matter here? Because the word placed in Nuh's mouth is *muslim*. The first Messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth was already commanded to be of the Muslims — and it is the last of the Messengers ﷺ who is now reciting that to the Quraysh.

## Ayah 73: the rescue, the ark, and the earth handed over

The whole flood arrives in a handful of words: *"They denied him, but We delivered him, and those with him in the ship, and We made them generations replacing one after another, while We drowned those who belied Our Ayat. Then see what was the end of those who were warned."*

**"Those with him"** — Ibn Kathir adds two words that change everything: *meaning, on his religion.* The verse does not identify the saved by tribe or standing. What it specifies is that they were on his religion. The ark is the community of faith made visible.

**"In the ship"** — the Arabic is *al-fulk*, and Ibn Kathir notes simply: **Fulk refers to the ark.**

**"We made them generations replacing one after another"** — *khalā'if*, and Ibn Kathir adds: **on earth.** This is the answer to the taunt of ayah 71. The people who found Nuh's presence unbearable are drowned; the small band who believed him become the successors on the earth, generation after generation. Nuh did not merely outlast his opponents — his community replaced theirs.

**"Then see what was the end of those who were warned."** Ibn Kathir reads the imperative as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: *"O Muhammad, see how We saved the believers and destroyed the deniers!"* The verse does not tell you what to feel; it tells you to **look**. Judge the two paths by where they ended.

And notice the phrase itself: the destroyed are called *"those who were warned."* They were not ambushed. They had a prophet living among them, reminding them, for as long as they found it unbearable.

## Ayah 74: the messengers after Nuh, and the sealed heart

*"Then after him We sent Messengers to their people. They brought them clear proofs, but they would not believe what they had already rejected beforehand. Thus We seal the hearts of the transgressors."*

Ibn Kathir reads the opening as: **then after Nuh We sent Messengers to their people**, and "they brought them clear proofs" as **evidences of the truth that they came with**.

Then the hinge: **"but they would not believe what they had already rejected beforehand"** means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that **the nations did not believe what their Messengers brought to them because they already rejected it from the beginning.** The first refusal was decisive. Evidence kept arriving — clear evidences of the truth — but the verdict had been passed before the evidence was heard. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: *"And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away"* (6:110).

**"Thus We seal the hearts of the transgressors."** Ibn Kathir draws out both directions of this sentence. Backwards: Allah set seals on the hearts of those people, such that they would not believe, **since they previously rejected faith**. Forwards: **He would also set seals on the hearts of the people that are like them, who will come after them** — and such people *"would not believe until they see the severe torment."*

Two things stand side by side in the wording. The sealing is ascribed to Allah — the verse says *We seal* — and it falls upon *al-muʿtadīn*, the transgressors. In Ibn Kathir's reading the order is clear: their rejection came first, and the seal followed it.

Ibn Kathir then states the historical upshot: **Allah destroyed the nations after Nuh — those that rejected the Messengers — and saved those who believed from among them.**

## The history behind the story

Ibn Kathir supplies the background that makes Nuh's mission intelligible: **from the time of Adam to Nuh, people followed Islam. Then they invented the worship of idols. So Allah sent Nuh to them.** Shirk is not humanity's starting point; it is a later invention laid over an original submission. **Ibn 'Abbas said: "There were ten generations between Adam and Nuh, and all of them were following Islam."**

That is why, Ibn Kathir notes, **on the Day of Resurrection the believers will say to Nuh: "You are the first Messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth."** The man being ridiculed in ayah 71 is the man the believers will one day address in those terms.

Ibn Kathir closes with the argument the passage was built to deliver, citing *"And how many generations have We destroyed after Nuh!"* (17:17). This was **a serious warning to the Arab pagans**, who rejected the leader and last of the Messengers and Prophets: if the people before them who rejected their Messengers had received this much punishment, *what did they think will happen to them since they perpetrated even greater sins than others before them?*

## Living it

- **Nuh's words are a script for anyone who has become inconvenient for telling the truth.** He states their grievance accurately, in their own terms; he declares his reliance on Allah; and, as Ibn Kathir puts it, he will not stop inviting them.
- **Reliance is not passivity.** *"Upon Allah I have placed my trust"* sits in the middle of the most confrontational speech in the passage. Tawakkul is what freed him to speak; it is not a reason to withdraw.
- **Ask nothing for the message.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is worth remembering exactly: *I have not asked you anything for my advice.* Sincerity is protected when there is nothing to lose by being refused.
- **"Those with him" meant those on his religion.** When the crisis actually came, that is the one thing the verse tells us about the people on the ark.
- **Guard the first refusal.** Ayah 74 warns about what happens when a person rejects the truth from the beginning: the clear proofs keep coming, and the heart has already stopped receiving.
- **Look at endings.** The instruction in ayah 73 is to see how Allah saved the believers and destroyed the deniers — to evaluate the two paths by where they finished.

passages.title: Moses before Pharaoh and the magicians' defeat
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** After the run of earlier messengers and their nations, ayat 75–82 turn to the confrontation between Musa and Harun, sent to Fir'awn, and the throne that met Allah's signs with the charge of "magic." Ibn Kathir titles the two halves of this passage "The Story of Musa and Fira'wn" and "Between Musa and the Magicians." One arc holds the eight ayat together: a message arrives with proofs; power refuses it out of arrogance rather than confusion; power escalates to a staged public contest; and Allah's word settles the matter — "And Allah will establish and make apparent the truth by His Words, however much the criminals may hate (it)" (82).

*A note on wording before we begin.* The Arabic word *siḥr* and its relatives run through the whole passage, but the translation quoted in Ibn Kathir's commentary renders it "magic" in ayat 76–77 and "sorcery" in ayat 79–81. They are the same word. Where quotations below alternate, that is the translator's variation, not two different things.

## The sending, and the verdict it met (75–76)

"Then after them We sent Musa and Harun to Fir'awn and his chiefs with Our Ayat. But they behaved arrogantly, and were a people who were criminals."

Ibn Kathir reads *thumma baʿathnā* — "Then after them We sent" — as meaning **"after these Messengers."** This is the next link in a chain, not an isolated episode. Two men are sent, not one. And they are sent to "Fir'awn and his chiefs," which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as **"his people."**

They come *bi-āyātinā*, "with Our Ayat," and Ibn Kathir explains this as **"Our proofs and evidences."** That gloss matters. An *āyah* here is not a spectacle laid on for entertainment; it is evidence tendered in an argument. Musa arrives as one who is making a case.

The response comes in two clauses that describe two different things, and Ibn Kathir separates them: "they behaved arrogantly" means **"they were too arrogant to follow the truth and submit to it,"** and beyond that arrogance, **"they were criminals."** So the failure is not intellectual. Nobody says the evidence was weak. They were too big, in their own estimation, to bow to it. Arrogance here is not a mood but a refusal — a refusal to submit to something you can see is true.

Then the labelling: "So, when came to them the truth from Us, they said: 'This is indeed clear magic.'" Notice what the ayah calls the thing before they do: **the truth**, and **from Us**. Allah names it correctly in the same breath in which He records their misnaming of it.

Notice too how they say it — "*indeed* … *clear* magic." The insistence is stacked on. Ibn Kathir catches the tone exactly: **"They were as if they gave an oath that what they had said was the truth. But they knew that what they were saying was a mere lie."** The louder the insistence, the emptier it was.

To show that they were lying against their own knowledge, Ibn Kathir cites Allah's verdict elsewhere in the Qur'an: **"And they belied them wrongfully and arrogantly, though they themselves were convinced thereof"** (27:14). Their inner certainty and their public statement pointed in opposite directions. That is a recognisable human disease: not "I have examined this and find it false," but "I cannot afford for this to be true."

## Musa's answer, and their three objections (77–78)

Ibn Kathir's own framing of ayah 77 is that **"Musa criticized them."** The reply is short, and it is all question: "Say you (this) about the truth when it has come to you? Is this magic? But the magicians will never be successful."

He does not begin by defending his own credentials. He makes them look again at the thing they have just labelled, and he refuses to adopt their vocabulary: he calls it *al-ḥaqq*, **the truth**, in the very sentence where they had called it magic. It is the same word Allah used of it in ayah 76 — and the same word that will close the passage in ayah 82.

The closing line, "the magicians will never be successful," is stated as a settled rule, not a prediction about one afternoon. And Ibn Kathir shows the same principle surfacing again at the height of the contest — this time from Allah Himself, addressing Musa: **"That which they have made is only a magician's trick, and the magician will never be successful, to whatever amount (of skill) he may attain"** (20:67–69). What Musa asserted as a principle, Allah confirms as His own judgement. No degree of skill changes the outcome; the problem with falsehood is not that it is badly executed.

Their answer in ayah 78 is three moves in one sentence, and they are still the standard three.

**First, inherited practice.** "Have you come to us to turn us away from that we found our fathers following?" Ibn Kathir spells out what "that we found our fathers following" means: **their religion.** Not an argument that the fathers were right — simply that the fathers were theirs. And the complaint is framed as being "turned away," as though the mere act of being redirected were the offence.

**Second, suspicion of motive.** "…and that you two may have greatness in the land?" Ibn Kathir glosses *al-kibriyāʼ*, rendered "greatness," as **"grandeur and leadership."** Men holding a throne accuse the messengers of wanting a throne — the very arrogance ayah 75 has just recorded as their own. When you cannot answer the message, question the messenger's ambitions.

**Third, the flat refusal.** "We are not going to believe you two!" No conditions, no test proposed. And the form is dual throughout — "you two," twice over. Harun, who says nothing in this passage, is being rejected just as fully as Musa.

## The festival Fir'awn staged (79–80)

"And Fir'awn said: 'Bring me every well-versed sorcerer.' And when the sorcerers came, Musa said to them: 'Cast down what you want to cast!'"

*Every* one — and every one of them well-versed. Having refused to believe, Fir'awn reaches for scale and for the resources of the state.

Ibn Kathir explains the strategy and its result plainly: **"Fir'awn, may Allah's curse be upon him, wanted to deceive the people and impress them with the tricks of the magicians in direct opposition to the plain truth that Musa brought. The result was the exact opposite and he therefore didn't attain his goal. The signs of the Lord prevailed in that public festival."**

Two details from Ibn Kathir make the scene human. First, the magicians **"stood in line after they received the promise of Fir'awn to become closer to him and obtain a generous reward"** — they came for access and for money. Second, Musa's own conduct in telling them to cast first: **"Musa wanted them to begin. He wanted the people to see what the magicians had made, then he would come with the truth after that to triumph over their falsehood."** That is not showmanship; it is the composure of someone who knows the outcome. Ibn Kathir cites the exchange: **"They said: 'O Musa! Either you throw first or we be the first to throw?' [Musa] said: 'Nay, throw you (first)!'"**

And then, honestly recorded, the hardest moment. Ibn Kathir says that when the magicians cast their spells **"they bewitched the eyes of the people through their display of mighty sorcery,"** and at that moment **"Musa conceived fear in himself"** — until Allah said to him: **"Fear not! Surely, you will have the upper hand. And throw that which is in your right hand! It will swallow up that which they have made"** (20:67–69). A prophet of Allah felt fear when falsehood looked overwhelming. The fear was not disbelief; it was met with reassurance, not rebuke.

Ibn Kathir also notes that this episode is told in Surat al-Aʿrāf — where he gives his fuller commentary on it — as well as in this surah, in Surat Ta Ha and in Surat ash-Shuʿarāʼ: different angles on one event.

## Two sentences that settle it (81–82)

Ibn Kathir places Musa's words immediately after Allah's reassurance: **"Upon that, Musa said: 'What you have brought is sorcery, Allah will surely make it of no effect. Verily, Allah does not set right the work of the evildoers.'"**

Musa names the thing accurately. *This* is magic — unlike the signs of Allah, which they had mislabelled in ayah 76. The sentence is a mirror held up to their accusation: the word they threw at revelation belongs, in fact, to what has just been produced in front of them.

And note the tense: "Allah **will** surely make it of no effect." He says it with the magicians' display still standing before a crowd whose eyes had been bewitched by it. He is not describing what he can see; he is announcing what Allah has already decided. And the agent is named — not "I will defeat it," but **"Allah will surely make it of no effect."**

The closing clause states the rule behind the ruling: **"Verily, Allah does not set right the work of the evildoers."** Allah will not lend His sustaining power to a project built to corrupt. It may glitter; it will not hold.

Then ayah 82, in the rendering Ibn Kathir's text carries: **"And Allah will establish and make apparent the truth by His Words, however much the criminals may hate (it)."**

Two things are worth feeling here. First, "establish **and make apparent**." The truth is not left to fend for itself, and it is not vindicated only in private; Allah brings it out into the open. Second, the means: *bi-kalimātihi*, **by His Words**. Not by Musa's eloquence, and not by the arithmetic of who had more men in the arena.

And "however much the criminals may hate it." *Al-mujrimūn* — the same word that closed ayah 75, where Fir'awn's people "were a people who were criminals," now closes the passage. Their hatred is acknowledged, and then dismissed as a factor. It changes nothing about the outcome; it is simply the weather the truth arrives in.

The end of the story, as Ibn Kathir gives it, is the perfect illustration. The very men Fir'awn had hired — brought in for nearness to him and a generous reward — **"fell down prostrate. They said: 'We believe in the Lord of all that exists – the Lord of Musa and Harun'"** (7:120–122). The instrument bought to bury the truth became the public evidence for it. Ibn Kathir's summary of Fir'awn is stark: **"Fir'awn thought that he would achieve victory through the magicians over the Messenger sent by Allah, the All-Knower of all hidden things. But he failed, lost Paradise and was deserving of the Hellfire."**

## A note carried over from ayah 64

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān material supplied alongside these ayat is not commentary on the Musa narrative; it is still completing an earlier discussion of ayah 64, where Allah promises the friends of Allah good news in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. Its explanation, in brief: the good news of the Hereafter comes at death, when the spirit is taken to Allah and he hears that Paradise is his, and again on the Day of Qiyamah when he rises from the grave to be welcomed to it. In support, it relates what al-Tabarani reported from Sayyidna Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said that people who recite *lā ilāha illā Allāh* will feel no fright at death, nor in the grave, nor when they rise from it — rising and shaking off the dust, saying, "Praised is Allah who has removed from us grief" (35:34). As for the good news in this world, the commentary cites the Prophet ﷺ, in a report of al-Bukhari from Sayyidna Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), that it is the true dreams a believer sees, or that are seen about him. And a further form of it: that Muslims at large love someone and think well of him with no personal motive — of which the Prophet ﷺ said that being thought well of is, for a true believer, good news received in ready cash (Muslim and al-Baghawi).

## Living it

**Learn the four moves, because they have not changed.** Call the truth by a dismissive name (76); appeal to what our fathers did (78); impute worldly ambition to whoever brings it (78); then bring in money and power to drown it out (79, with the promise of nearness and reward). Recognising the pattern keeps you from being unsettled by it.

**Do not mistake arrogance for a question.** Ibn Kathir's point on ayat 75–76 is that Fir'awn's circle knew: they spoke as though swearing an oath, while knowing that what they said was a lie. Some resistance to truth is a genuine search for evidence and deserves patient answering; some is a refusal to submit, and no further evidence will help. Musa answered anyway — but he answered by naming the truth accurately, not by begging for approval.

**Let the truth be tested.** Musa deliberately invited his opponents to go first, in public, on their strongest ground, because he wanted the people to see what they had made before the truth came after it. Confidence in what Allah has revealed does not need to control the conditions of the contest.

**Fear is allowed; despair is not.** Musa conceived fear in himself when the crowd's eyes had been bewitched, and Allah's answer was "Fear not! Surely, you will have the upper hand." If a prophet's heart could tighten at the sight of falsehood on parade, ours may too. The remedy is the same: what Allah has decided is not adjusted by how impressive the opposition looks.

**Anchor your certainty in ayah 82, not in the scoreboard.** Falsehood is often louder, better funded, better staffed, and ahead on the day. Ayah 81 tells us who makes it of no effect, and ayah 82 tells us who establishes and makes truth apparent — Allah, by His Words. Our task is to bring the *āyāt* — the proofs and evidences — and to say the true thing accurately. The establishing is His.

passages.title: The few who believed and their prayer
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** After all the clear signs Musa (peace be upon him) brought, ayah 83 delivers a quiet, devastating piece of arithmetic: hardly anyone believed. Ayat 84–86 then show what that small, frightened group did with the faith they had. Musa turns them toward reliance on Allah, and they answer him with a *duʿāʾ* — a supplication, a calling upon Allah. The four ayat move as one arc: **fear** (83), **the call to trust** (84), and **the words of trust, and the duʿāʾ that follows them** (85–86).

## Ayah 83: belief held in a state of fear

The word the translation before you renders as "a few youths of his people" is the word *dhurriyyah*, which Ibn Kathir renders "the offspring of his people." Whichever shade you take, the point is the same: a handful, not a movement.

And they believed **ʿalā khawf**. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the phrase spells out what that fear was: "because of the fear of Firʿawn and his chiefs, lest they should persecute them." They were not merely nervous; in Ibn Kathir's words they were "even scared that Firʿawn and his followers would force them to return to *Kufr* (disbelief)."

Then the ayah names the reason for that fear: **"and verily, Firʿawn was an arrogant tyrant on the earth, he was indeed one of the transgressors."** Ibn Kathir comments simply: "Firʿawn was an evil tyrant and extremely arrogant. His people feared him and his power too much."

That is worth sitting with. The obstacle to faith here was not a lack of evidence. Ibn Kathir is explicit that this tiny response came "despite all the clear signs and irrefutable evidence Musa came with." The obstacle was a man, and the fear of a man.

## Who were the few?

Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas an explanation that changes the picture entirely. The offspring who believed in Musa, he said, were **from Firʿawn's people, other than Banu Israel — and they were few.** Ibn ʿAbbas names some of them:

- **Firʿawn's wife**
- **the believer who was hiding his faith**
- **Firʿawn's treasurer**
- **and his wife**

So the few who believed were not the oppressed underclass — they were people inside the tyrant's own household and administration. His wife. The man who handled his wealth. Faith reached the innermost rooms of the palace, and even there, as the list itself records, one of them is simply "the believer who was hiding his faith."

As for the Children of Israel, Ibn Kathir says, they "themselves believed in Musa, **all of them**. They were glad to see him coming. They knew of his description and the news of his advent from their previous Books. They knew that Allah was going to save them through him from the capture of Firʿawn and give them power over him."

On this reading, ayah 83 is not saying the Israelites refused Musa; it is measuring how few of *Firʿawn's* people broke ranks.

## Firʿawn's precautions did not help him

Ibn Kathir adds a detail that reads almost as a commentary on tyranny itself. When this knowledge reached Firʿawn, "he was very wary. But his caution and weariness didn't help him one bit." Instead, "When Musa arrived, Firʿawn subjected them to great harm" — and Ibn Kathir cites their complaint and Musa's answer:

> "They said: 'We (Children of Israel) suffered troubles before you came to us, and since you have come to us.' He said: 'It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors on the earth, so that He may see how you act.'" (7:129)

Notice the shape of Musa's reply. He does not promise them ease; the promise of relief arrives with a purpose attached — "so that He may see how you act."

## Ayah 84: "then put your trust in Him"

Into that pressure Musa speaks: **"O my people! If you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him if you are Muslims."**

Notice how the ayah is worded. The command to rely on Allah is set between two mentions of what they already profess — *if you have believed in Allah* in front of it, and *if you are Muslims*, that is, submitters, behind it. The instruction is addressed to people on the basis of the faith they say they have.

*Tawakkul* is the Arabic word behind "put your trust" — reliance, entrusting the outcome to Allah; Ibn Kathir's own summary word for it is "reliance." And his answer to the unspoken question *but is that enough?* is one line: **"Allah is sufficient for those who put their trust in Him."** He then lets the Qurʾan answer for itself:

> **"Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?"** (39:36)
> **"And whosoever puts his trust in Allah, then He will suffice him."** (65:3)

Then Ibn Kathir makes a broader observation that is one of the most useful things in the whole passage: **"Allah combines worship and reliance in many places."** He gathers them:

> **"So worship Him and put your trust in Him."** (11:123)
> **"Say: 'He is the Most Gracious (Allah), in Him we believe, and in Him we put our trust.'"** (67:29)
> **"(He alone is) the Lord of the east and the west; none has the right to be worshipped but He. So take Him (alone) as a protector."** (73:9)

And he ends the list where every Muslim lives: **"And Allah commanded the believers to say many times in their Salah: 'You (Alone) we worship, and You (Alone) we ask for help.'" (1:5)**

Worship and reliance, paired again and again — and, as Ibn Kathir points out, placed on our tongues many times in the prayer itself.

## Ayat 85–86: the answer

Musa said **fa-ʿalayhi tawakkalū** — "then put your trust in Him." They replied **ʿalā Allahi tawakkalnā** — "In Allah we put our trust." Ibn Kathir describes it exactly so: "The Children of Israel **complied with this command** and said…"

And in the same breath in which they declare their reliance, they ask. Their trust and their petition sit inside one sentence.

### "Our Lord! Make us not a trial for the folk who are wrongdoers"

*Fitnah* is the Arabic word rendered here as "a trial"; it appears again untranslated in Mujahid's reported meaning below, "make us fall into *Fitnah*." But a trial for whom? Ibn Kathir reports two meanings.

**First meaning — do not let us become a proof for their falsehood.** Ibn Kathir explains: "This means don't give them victory over us so that they rule us. So they might not think that they have authority over us because they were following the truth and we were falsehood. This might be a deceiving trial for them." He notes that this meaning **was reported from Abu Mijliz and Abu Ad-Duha.**

Read it slowly, because it is a remarkable thing to pray. These people are hunted, hiding their faith, afraid of being forced back into disbelief — and this request is not *spare us*. It is: *do not let our defeat become the thing that persuades the oppressor he was right all along.* Their concern, as Ibn Kathir words it, is the wrongdoers' own deceiving trial — the false conclusion the tyrant would draw about truth and falsehood.

**Second meaning — do not let them break us.** ʿAbdur-Razzaq, in a narration from **Mujahid**, gives the meaning as: "Do not give them authority over us so they might make us fall into *Fitnah*." That is, do not put us under their power in a way that pulls us out of our faith. This runs straight back to ayah 83, where their fear was precisely that they would be forced to return to *Kufr*.

Ibn Kathir records both without setting one against the other. Both begin from the same request — *do not give them power over us* — and differ over what is chiefly feared in the outcome: the wrongdoers' deceiving trial, or the believers' own fall into fitnah.

### "And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving folk"

The final ayah is the plainest and the most tender. Ibn Kathir glosses **"and save us by Your mercy"** as: "save us **through Your mercy and beneficence**."

They do not say *save us because we deserve it*, or *because we were the only ones brave enough to believe*. Having just declared their trust, they name the one thing they are counting on: His mercy and His beneficence.

And **"from the disbelieving folk"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning "from **those who denied the truth and covered it**." Both verbs are his: denied, and covered.

Ibn Kathir closes the passage with the believers' own final posture: **"We truly have believed in You and put our trust in You."**

## Living it

Read as one unit, these four ayat give a working portrait of faith under pressure:

- **Being few is not evidence of being wrong.** Ayah 83 records that the truth once had a handful of adherents while an arrogant tyrant held the state.
- **Fear does not cancel faith.** They believed *ʿalā khawf*, in fear of Firʿawn and his chiefs. Allah records their belief without erasing their fear. What Musa teaches them next is where to put their weight.
- **The command comes addressed to what you already claim.** *If you have believed in Allah… if you are Muslims* — that is the frame Musa places around "put your trust in Him."
- **Worship and reliance travel together**, as Ibn Kathir showed across 11:123, 67:29, 73:9 and 1:5 — and, he notes, Allah commanded the believers to say that pairing many times in their Salah: *You (Alone) we worship, and You (Alone) we ask for help.*
- **Trust, and ask.** Ayat 85–86 place the duʿāʾ right beside the declaration of trust — and the duʿāʾ asks for mercy, not for reward.
- **Pray for your steadfastness, not only your comfort.** Their request is that they not be made a *fitnah* — on one reported meaning, that they not be made to fall into fitnah themselves; on the other, that their defeat not become a deceiving trial for the wrongdoers.

## A closing note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼan

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼan material carried with this section comments on the earlier statement in this surah (ayah 64) that, for the friends of Allah, there is **good news in the worldly life and in the Hereafter** — a fitting horizon for a frightened few who were told to rely on their Lord.

As for the good news of the Hereafter, Maʿārif ul Qurʼan says it comes at the time of death, when the deceased hears the good news that Paradise is for him, and again on the Day of Qiyamah when he rises from his grave and is welcomed to Paradise. It cites a narration reported by **al-Tabarani** from Sayyidna Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said that people who recite *la ilaha illallah* will not experience any fright at the time of death, nor inside the grave, nor at the time they rise from it — and he described seeing them rise, shaking the dust off, saying: **"Praised is Allah who has removed from us all grief"** (35:34).

As for the good news in this world, Maʿārif ul Qurʼan mentions two forms. The Prophet ﷺ explained it as **the true dreams** a person sees himself, or that someone else sees with him in them (reported by **al-Bukhari** from Sayyidna Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him). And there is the good news that Muslims at large love someone and take him to be good, without any personal motive or interest — of which the Prophet ﷺ said that being taken as good and praiseworthy is, for a true Muslim, good news **in ready cash** (Muslim and al-Baghawi).

For a believer living in fear, that is a promise worth holding on to: the fright ends, the grief is removed, and — as Ibn Kathir said of this very ayah — "Allah is sufficient for those who put their trust in Him."

passages.title: Houses of worship and Moses' answered prayer
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat move from the smallest, most private act of a hunted community — praying behind a closed door — to the largest public verdict passed on their oppressor.** Ayah 87 is an instruction for survival: when Fir'awn makes worship in the usual places impossible, worship goes indoors. Ayah 88 is the prayer Musa (peace be upon him) made after he had lost all hope of reforming Fir'awn's people. Ayah 89 is Allah's answer — and, in the same breath, a command to the two brothers to keep walking straight while that answer takes its time. What holds the passage together is one thread: **the believer's duty does not stop when circumstances close in, and it does not stop once the du'a has been accepted.**

## Why a house had to become a mosque

To feel ayah 87 you need the situation behind it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays it out. The Children of Israel, who followed the religious law of Musa (peace be upon him), performed their prayers **only in their synagogues**, as was customary. This was not merely custom: the earlier communities were bound by this injunction, and their prayers were not valid if performed in their homes. Fir'awn used to oppress them in all sorts of ways, and realizing this about their law, he had all the synagogues demolished — so that they would be deprived of offering their prayers in accordance with their religious law.

It is at that point that Allah sent this instruction to the two prophets of Bani Isra'il, Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both): new houses were to be built in Egypt for Bani Isra'il, oriented towards the Qiblah, so that the prayers could be offered in those very residential houses.

Ibn Kathir preserves the same picture from the earliest authorities, and adds the note of fear that runs beneath it. Al-'Awfi reported that Ibn 'Abbas said the Children of Israel told Musa, "We cannot offer our prayers in public in front of Fir'awn's people." So Allah permitted them to pray in their houses, and they were commanded to build those houses in the direction of the Qiblah. Mujahid puts the danger more starkly: when Banu Israel feared that Fir'awn might kill them **in their gatherings at their temples**, they were commanded to take their houses as places of worship — facing the Qiblah, and **the prayer could be in secret**. Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak stated the same.

So this is not a general licence. It is a concession issued under siege, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful about its limits (citing *Ruh al-Ma'ani*): it can also be said that even at that time of emergency the permission was for particular houses oriented towards the Qiblah — praying in common homes and public places was still not permitted. The Muslim community, by contrast, has the convenience of offering prayers anywhere, be it a city or wilderness.

## The convenience we inherited

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws that contrast explicitly through a hadith. In a hadith of **Sahih Muslim**, the Holy Prophet ﷺ mentions, among six things given uniquely to him, *the whole earth has been made a masjid for me* — meaning that Salah performed anywhere remains valid.

That freedom does not flatten everything, though. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes two refinements that sit alongside it: performing the obligatory prayers **in congregation in the masjids** has been declared an emphasised Sunnah; and voluntary (nafl) prayers are **better said inside the home**. This was the usual practice of the Holy Prophet ﷺ — he would say only the Fard Salah (the obligatory prayer, the one every Muslim owes five times a day) in the masjid, then go home and say his Sunnahs and nawafil there.

There is a quiet lesson in that pairing. Bani Isra'il were driven into their homes by a tyrant; we are invited into ours by a Sunnah. The house that becomes a place of prayer is, in either case, a house that changes character.

## What the verse proves about Salah itself

Two conclusions are drawn from ayah 87 in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:

- **Facing the Qiblah was a condition of prayer during the period of the past prophets too** — the command to orient the houses would be meaningless otherwise.
- Alongside it, it stands proved from authentic reports that **purity (taharah)** and **covering the body (satr al-'awrah)** were likewise conditions of Salah in the religious laws of all the past prophets.

These are not innovations of our sharia. They are the enduring grammar of standing before Allah.

## Which Qiblah did they face?

A natural question, and the sources meet it head-on. Which Qiblah were Bani Isra'il told to face — the Ka'bah, or Baytu 'l-Maqdis?

**Sayyidna 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas** (may Allah be pleased with him) said it means **the Ka'bah**, and that the Ka'bah alone was the Qiblah of Musa (peace be upon him) and his people — as reported in al-Qurtubi and *Ruh al-Ma'ani*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some religious scholars say the real Qiblah of **all** the past prophets was none other than the Ka'bah.

What, then, of the report that the Jews turn their faces towards the Sakhrah (the Rock) of Baytu 'l-Maqdis during their prayers? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves it by period: it is applied to the time **after** Musa (peace be upon him) left Egypt and headed towards Baytu 'l-Maqdis, which is not contrary to the Baytullah being his Qiblah during the period of his stay in Egypt.

## A shift in who is being addressed

Read ayah 87 slowly and you will notice the addressee changing three times — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows that each shift is deliberate:

1. **Dual** at the start — *"We revealed to Musa and his brother"* — because the two of them together were charged with the responsibility of having the houses made Qiblah-oriented and allowing the occupants to pray in them.
2. **Plural** in the middle — *"establish the Salah"* — the plural form including all Bani Isra'il, because this law included everyone, the prophet and his community alike.
3. **Singular** at the end — *"and give glad tidings to the believers"* — given particularly to Musa (peace be upon him), because it was he, as the law-giving prophet, who had the right to give out the good news of Paradise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws out why "establish Salah" follows the command about the houses at all. Since the very purpose of making the houses Qiblah-oriented was to pray in them, the sequence is itself the ruling: *if the Pharaoh stops you from making prayers in places reserved for worship, prayers do not stand dropped — make them in your homes.* A tyrant can take your building. He cannot take your Salah.

And the glad tidings at the close, according to *Ruh al-Ma'ani*: that their mission will be successful, that they will overpower the enemy, and that in the Hereafter they will go to Paradise. A people who may pray only in secret are told, in the same verse, that they will win.

## Ayah 88: the prayer of a prophet who had run out of hope

**"Our Lord! You have indeed bestowed on Fir'awn and his chiefs splendour and wealth in the life of this world…"**

Ibn Kathir glosses **zīnah** as the splendour and pleasure of this worldly life, and **amwāl** as wealth plentiful and abundant. Al-Qurtubi, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is more concrete still: mines of gold, silver and precious stones in Egypt and Ethiopia.

Notice how Musa (peace be upon him) frames it — as a complaint about the **effect that wealth had on other people**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the mechanism precisely: as a result of that splendour they misled people from Allah's way, because when ordinary people looked at their bulging affluence they started doubting — *had they been in error, why would they have been so blessed?* Ordinary people were unable to see through to the reality that material affluence without good deeds cannot be the sign of a person being right and true. And it was only after being disappointed in his efforts to correct Fir'awn's people, and realizing the danger their glamour and wealth posed to others who were being misled by it, that Musa (peace be upon him) invoked this prayer.

### Two readings of "so that they lead astray"

Ibn Kathir records that this phrase was read in two ways, and each opens a different meaning:

- With a **fatḥah** over the yā' (*li-yaḍillū*, "so that they themselves go astray"): "You have given them that while You know they would not believe in what You have sent me with to them. You did that so they would gradually be drawn away from the truth." Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's words *"that We may test them thereby"* (20:131 and 72:17) — wealth given as a test that draws its holder gradually away from the truth.
- With a **ḍammah** over the yā' (*li-yuḍillū*, "so that they lead others astray"): You have given them that so whoever You willed among Your creatures will be tried; those whom You wish to misguide would think You gave it to them because You loved them and cared about them.

Both readings land on the same warning from opposite ends: prosperity is not a certificate of divine approval — not for the one who holds it, and not in the eyes of the one who watches him hold it.

### "Our Lord, obliterate their wealth"

On *"Our Lord! Destroy their wealth"*, Ibn Kathir reports two lines of interpretation. **Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid** said they asked Allah to destroy their wealth. **Ad-Dahhak, Abu al-'Aliyah and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas** said Allah made their wealth into engraved stones as it was before.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills this in from **Sayyidna Qatadah** (may Allah be pleased with him): such was the effect of this invocation that all the gold, precious coins, stones and land produce belonging to Fir'awn's people were transformed into bland rock. It adds a striking detail — in a bag found during the period of the pious Khalifah **'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz**, there were things dating back to the time of the Pharaoh, and among them were eggs and almonds of solid rock. Leading commentators say Allah turned all the fruits, vegetables and grains they had into rock. And this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is among the **nine clear signs** given to Musa mentioned in *"and We gave Musa nine clear signs"* (17:101).

Think about what that punishment actually is. The eggs and almonds kept their shape; what they had lost was every particle of worth. The affluence that had made onlookers doubt was left standing in form and emptied of value.

### "And harden their hearts" — the difficult half

The second half of the du'a is harder: *"and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful torment."* Ibn 'Abbas explained "harden their hearts" as meaning **put a seal on them**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the objection openly rather than avoiding it: such an invocation obviously appears far out as coming through the speech of a prophet, because the sole mission of a prophet's life is nothing but to invite people to believe and act right and to make efforts towards that end.

Two answers come from the sources.

**Ibn Kathir:** this prayer was from Musa *because he was angry for the sake of Allah and His religion*. He prayed against Fir'awn and his chiefs **when he was certain that there was no good in them**. Ibn Kathir then places beside it, with the word "Similarly," the prayer of Nuh (peace be upon him): *"My Lord! Leave not one of the disbelievers on the earth! If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants, and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers."* (71:26–27).

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān:** in terms of the hard facts of the situation, Musa (peace be upon him) had already made whatever efforts he could and was totally disappointed. What he now wanted was that they learn through the punishment for their deeds — and in doing so it was probable that these people, once they saw the punishment coming, might make a confession and declare that they now believed, whereby the punishment could stand warded off. So what became the cause of this invocation was **his hatred for kufr** (disbelief), not a desire for their ruin.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is similar to what happened to the Pharaoh himself: when he started to announce his belief at the time he was drowning, the angel Jibra'il shut his mouth lest divine mercy turn to him and he stand delivered from the punishment.

## Ayah 89: "the prayer of you both"

Allah's response comes in the dual: **"Verily, the invocation of you both is accepted."** Ibn Kathir explains the acceptance as being in destroying Fir'awn's people.

But why *both*, when only Musa was speaking? Because — as both commentaries record — while Musa (peace be upon him) was making this prayer, **Harun (peace be upon him) kept saying Āmīn**. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: Harun said "Amin" to his brother's prayer, and Allah answered Musa's prayer.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two practical points from this:

- **Saying Āmīn is itself part of the prayer.** Harun was taken as associated with the act of prayer, and so the address came as "the prayer of you both has been granted." That is a remarkable dignity conferred on a single word.
- Since the method of du'a given in the Holy Qur'an is to make it **in a lowered voice**, saying Āmīn in a lowered mode too seems preferable.

## "So stand firm" — and the forty years

Then comes the instruction that makes this passage so useful to anyone who has ever prayed and waited: *"so stand firm, and never follow the way of those who do not know."*

Ibn Kathir: as I have answered your prayer, you should remain steadfast on My command. Ibn Jurayj narrated that Ibn 'Abbas said about this ayah: **"Be steadfast and follow My command."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why steadfastness needed mentioning at precisely this moment.
