The two prophets were informed that the prayer was accepted — yet even they were somewhat tested, because according to **al-Baghawi** the effect of that prayer unfolded **after forty years**. Acceptance was announced; the visible result was four decades away. That is why the news of acceptance is followed immediately by *stand firm and do not follow the way of those who do not know*: they should go on carrying the mission of calling people to the true faith, and **not get embarrassed, disappointed or hasty like the ignorant when the effects of the acceptance of some prayer take their due time**.

## Living it

The passage leaves a believer with three concrete things.

**When worship gets squeezed, it relocates — it does not lapse.** The synagogues came down and the prayer continued in the houses. Whatever takes away your usual place of worship has not taken away the obligation, and the sequence in ayah 87 — orient the houses, *then* establish the Salah — says so directly: prayers do not stand dropped.

**Do not read wealth as a verdict.** Both readings in ayah 88 warn against the same illusion from different angles: the affluence of a wrongdoer misleads onlookers into thinking he must be favoured, and misleads him into thinking the same. Material affluence without good deeds cannot be the sign of a person being right and true.

**A prayer answered is not a prayer completed.** Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) were told "the prayer of you both has been granted" and in the next words told to stand firm and not follow the way of those who do not know. Forty years passed. If the two of them were told to keep carrying the mission after a guaranteed answer, then the delay between our du'a and its effect is not evidence of rejection — it is the space in which steadfastness is meant to happen.

passages.title: Pharaoh's drowning and Israel's settlement
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close the story of Musa and Fir'awn by setting its two endings side by side: the tyrant drowned in the sea he had claimed a right to, and the people he had pursued in oppression and enmity brought safely across it and settled in an honourable dwelling place.

What binds the passage together is one question: **when is it too late?** Ayah 90 shows Fir'awn believing; ayah 91 shows that belief being refused; ayah 92 turns his corpse into a public sign — and then notes that most people still take no lesson from signs; ayah 93 shows the honour Allah gave the Children of Israel, and how they too, once knowledge reached them, fell into disputes.

## The crossing: the scene Ibn Kathir sets

Ibn Kathir fills in the moment. The Children of Israel left Egypt in the company of Musa — it was said there were six hundred thousand soldiers, plus their offspring. They had borrowed a great deal of ornaments from the Coptics and taken it with them. Fir'awn became very angry and sent heralds to all the cities to send their soldiers, then set out behind them "filled with great pride and with massive armies."

Ibn Kathir pauses on a detail worth noticing: **no one who had any authority or power remained behind in Fir'awn's kingdom.** The whole apparatus of the state marched into the trap. "Allah wanted this to happen," he says, "for He had a plan for them."

They caught up with the Israelites at sunrise. Trapped between the army and the water, Musa's people said, *"We are sure to be overtaken"* (26:61), and kept asking him how they could be saved that day. Musa answered that he had been commanded to come this way, and then said the words that turn the whole scene: ***"Nay, verily, with me is my Lord. He will guide me"*** (26:62).

Ibn Kathir's comment is one line: *it had been so difficult, but it suddenly became easy.* Musa was commanded to strike the sea with his staff; it was cleft asunder, each part standing like a mighty mountain — twelve paths, one for each Israelite tribe — and Allah commanded the wind so the path was dry underfoot, as in *"strike a dry path for them in the sea, fearing neither to be overtaken nor being afraid"* (20:77). The water between the paths appeared as windows, so each tribe could see the others and not think they had been destroyed.

When the last Israelite had crossed, Fir'awn and his soldiers arrived at the edge of the far shore — a hundred thousand black horses in addition to horsemen of other colours. **Seeing the sea, Fir'awn was frightened and wanted to turn back.** But, says Ibn Kathir, it was too late: Allah's decree had prevailed and Musa's prayer had been answered. Jibril came on a war stallion, passed by Fir'awn's horse — his horse whinnied at Fir'awn's — and rushed into the sea; Fir'awn did the same behind him. He no longer had any control over matters — yet still, wanting to sound strong before his chiefs, he declared that the Children of Israel had no greater right to the sea than he did. Mika'il came behind their army, pushing them all in.

When they were all in the sea and the first of them was about to emerge on the other side, Allah commanded the sea to strand them. It closed over them, and none was saved.

## The confession that came too late (ayah 90)

The waves accumulated above Fir'awn and he was overwhelmed by the stupors of death. It was in that state, Ibn Kathir says, that he spoke the words of ayah 90: *"I believe that none has the right to be worshipped but He in Whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am one of the Muslims."*

Note the wording: even here, he names Allah only as *the One the Children of Israel believe in* — the very people he had been pursuing in oppression and enmity moments before. Ibn Kathir sums it up without ceremony: **"He believed at a time when he couldn't benefit from his faith."** This is not an exception but a law, and Ibn Kathir cites the Qur'an's own statement of it — *"Then their faith could not avail them when they saw Our punishment. This has been the way of Allah in dealing with His servants"* (40:84–85).

Ibn Kathir adds something easy to skim past: these facts about Fir'awn — what he said, and his status at that moment — **were among the secrets of the Unseen that Allah revealed to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ.** The sea had left no survivor to report them.

**From the Sunnah.** Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: *"Jibril said to me: If you could have seen me while I was taking black mud from the sea and placing it into the mouth of Fir'awn, out of fear that the mercy would reach him."* Abu 'Isa At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir also recorded it; At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Gharib Sahih."

## "Now?" — the door that had already shut (ayah 91)

Ayah 91 is Allah's own reply, and it lands like a door closing: *"Now — when you disobeyed before, and you were one of the mischief-makers?"* Ibn Kathir paraphrases: *do you say that just now, when you have disobeyed Allah before that?* And "the mischief-makers" (**al-mufsidīn**) means, he says, that Fir'awn was among the makers of mischief on the earth **who misled the people** — which is why the Qur'an elsewhere speaks of such men as those *"made leaders inviting to the Fire; and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped"* (28:41). He did not merely lose himself; he took a nation with him.

### The ruling this ayah establishes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the legal principle out plainly: **a profession of faith made exactly at the time of death is not legally trustworthy.** It cites the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah keeps accepting a servant's repentance until the time of the *ghargharah* of death arrives (Tirmidhi).

*Ghargharah* is the death-rattle — the time the soul is being drawn out of the body, when the angels appear face to face. At that point, explains Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, life in this world, the home of deeds, is all over, and the laws of the Hereafter come into force. **Nothing done then is acceptable — neither belief nor disbelief.** Whoever believes at that time will not be called a believer, and will not be treated as one in shrouding and burial. Fir'awn's fate is the proof: there is a consensus that he died a disbeliever, and this is also what the text of the Qur'an says. If anyone is reported to have called Pharaoh's belief valid, that report is either given a suitable interpretation or else the statement is considered false (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī).

The principle cuts both ways, and mercifully so. If a person were to utter a word of disbelief while the soul is being drawn out, **he is not thereby called a disbeliever**: the funeral prayer is offered for him, he is buried like Muslims, and his words are interpreted in his favour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this has happened in the case of some of the *awliyāʼ* — friends of Allah whose utterances bothered those around them, until they became conscious and explained, and everyone realised it had been nothing but a declaration of true belief.

**But do not try to live on that deadline.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends with a warning to those who witness this transition from one world to the other: it is possible to make a mistake in determining the correct situation. Is this the drawing of the soul from the body (*nazʿ al-rūḥ*)? The last rattle of death (*ghargharah*)? Or the agony that prevails earlier, while repentance is still accepted? Nothing done at that time is valid in terms of the Sharīʿah — but everything is, if done before it. The line itself is invisible, which is exactly why repentance is a thing for today.

## The body kept as an exhibit (ayah 92)

*"So this day We shall deliver your body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you."* Ibn Kathir glosses *nunajjīka* — "We shall deliver you" — as meaning *We will put your body on a high place on the earth*, and Mujahid explains *bi-badanik* as **your physical body**. The word of rescue is used, and what it rescues is a corpse.

Why? Ibn 'Abbas and others from among the Salaf — the earliest generations of Muslims — explained: **some of the Children of Israel doubted the death of Fir'awn.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the psychology — when Musa told them after the crossing that Pharaoh had drowned, they had been so overawed and subdued by that man that they refused to believe the news and said he was not drowned. So Allah commanded the sea to throw his body up — whole, without a soul, with his known armour plate — onto a high place on the land where everyone could see it.

So the sign works on two levels, as Ibn Kathir has it: proof to the Children of Israel of his death and destruction, and proof **that Allah is All-Powerful, in Whose control are all the creatures, and that nothing can bear His anger.**

**The day it happened.** Fir'awn and his people were destroyed on the day of 'Ashura'. Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn 'Abbas: when the Prophet ﷺ arrived at Al-Madinah he found the Jews fasting that day and asked, *"What is this day that you are fasting?"* They responded, "This is the day in which Musa was victorious over Fir'awn." So the Prophet ﷺ said: *"You have more right to Musa than they, so fast it."*

**About the mummy.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the place where the body was found is still known as the mount of Pharaoh, and that after that it is not known what ultimately became of the corpse. It mentions newspaper reports of a pharaoh's body found intact, seen by the public and deposited in the Cairo Museum — but cautions that **it cannot be said with certainty that this is the same Pharaoh who confronted Musa**, since every ruler of Egypt in that period had the title of Pharaoh and their names differ. Its conclusion is measured: the same Divine power that threw a drowned body ashore may well have kept it preserved against spoilage so that it could become a lesson for future generations, and it may still be there — *however, it remains essential to learn a lesson from it rather than to become excited about its discovery as an archaeological triumph.*

**"And verily, many among mankind are heedless of Our Ayat."** Notice that the same word covers both halves of the lesson: the corpse is an **āyah**, a sign, and Allah's revealed verses are His **āyāt**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that people do not ponder over them and so fail to learn their essential lesson in living a better life — otherwise signs abound, everywhere, in every particle of this universe, and a look at them would help a person recognise Allah and His perfect power. A preserved body behind museum glass proves nothing to a heedless eye.

## The other ending: Israel settled and provided for (ayah 93)

Against the tyrant's end, ayah 93 brings into focus the future of a people bulldozed in disgrace by the Pharaoh. Ibn Kathir reads it as an inventory of all the worldly and religious gifts Allah bestowed upon the Children of Israel.

**"An honourable dwelling place" — *mubawwaʼ ṣidq*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ṣidq* here means good and proper: a place suited to them in every way. Ibn Kathir reports that it means Egypt and Syria around Jerusalem, as it was said by some. When Allah destroyed Fir'awn and his soldiers, the Mosaic State took control of all of Egypt — *"And We made the people who were considered weak to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts thereof which We have blessed... because of their endurance"* (7:137); *"So We expelled them from gardens and springs, treasures, and every kind of honourable place — thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them"* (26:57–59). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that they were then given the holy lands of Jordan and Palestine, which Allah had assigned to Sayyidnā Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his progeny as their inheritance.

That inheritance, Ibn Kathir notes, was not instant. Continuing with Musa to seek Jerusalem — the land of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah — they found giant people there and refrained from fighting them, so Allah expelled them into the wilderness for forty years. During that time first Harun died, then Musa; Yushaʿ bin Nun led after them, and Allah supported them to conquer Jerusalem and rule it for a period of time.

**"And provided them with good things" — *min al-ṭayyibāt*.** Ibn Kathir defines this as provision that is **lawful, pure and useful — good both in nature and in the Law**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds simply: they had the best of everything.

## "They did not differ until the knowledge came to them"

This is the sting in the ayah. Ibn Kathir's reading: **there should have been no reason for them to have any disputes among them**, since Allah had sent them knowledge and explained matters and issues to them. Knowledge should have ended argument; instead it became the occasion for it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it specifically. Among them too there were many who, soon after having power, failed to appreciate the blessings of Allah and went about disobeying Him. They recited the Torah and knew from it the signs and marks of the Prophet ﷺ. That awareness demanded that they should have been the first to believe in him as soon as he came. And in fact **they believed in his coming before he actually came** — telling people the signs he would have and the time he would come, even using his *wasīlah* (medium) in their prayers. Then he came with a whole array of evidences of his veracity and the very signs identified in the Torah — and at that point they started disputing among themselves: some believed, the rest refused.

That is why, on this reading, "the knowledge came to them" expresses *the coming of the Prophet ﷺ to them*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two further readings of *ʿilm* here: it could also denote **certitude** — so that once the causes of observation and certitude converged, the disputing began; or, as some commentators have said, *ʿilm* (knowledge) stands for *maʿlūm* (the known one) — that is, when the blessed person already known through the prophecies of the Torah came before them face to face, they started disputing the truth.

**A warning that includes us.** Ibn Kathir cites here the hadith: *"The Jews separated into seventy-one sects, and the Christians separated into seventy-two sects, and this Ummah will separate into seventy-three sects, one of which is in Paradise, seventy-two in the Fire."* They asked, "Who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He replied: *"Those upon what I and my Companions are upon."* It was recorded by Al-Hakim in his *Mustadrak* with this wording. The pattern of ayah 93 — knowledge arriving, then division — is not a foreign disease.

**The verdict is deferred, not cancelled.** *"Verily your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that in which they used to differ."* Ibn Kathir explains that "judge" here means **to distinguish between them** — to separate the parties. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: on that Day truth will become distinct from falsehood, and the upholders of truth will be sent to Paradise, the practitioners of falsehood to Hell. Disputes that could not be settled by evidence in this world are not lost; they are held over for a Judge who will not be misled.

## Living it

**Repent while repentance still counts.** The faith Fir'awn grabbed at in the last seconds had been open to him his whole life. The deadline is real, but — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns — nobody can see exactly where it falls. Everything before the *ghargharah* is accepted; therefore, now.

**Watch what your position does to you.** Fir'awn was frightened at the water's edge and wanted to turn back — and once he was in it, with no control over matters left to him, what he still reached for was a show of strength before his chiefs. Even then, the audience mattered more to him than the truth.

**Do not mistake knowledge for safety.** Ayah 93 is about a people who were rescued, settled, provided from the good things, and given clear knowledge — and who split apart precisely when the truth arrived. Knowledge does not protect you; acting on it does.

**Take the lesson, not the spectacle.** Whether or not the body in the museum is his, ayah 92 has already told you what it is for — and warned, in the same breath, that many people will look straight at a sign and register nothing.

passages.title: Doubt, the earlier scriptures, and settled denial
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah speaks directly to the Prophet ﷺ: if there were any doubt about what has been sent down, then ask the people who have been reading the Book before him. The translation glosses the object of that doubt as "˹these stories˺" — and Ibn Kathir, commenting on these verses, points back to an account earlier in this same surah, where Musa (peace be upon him) prays against Fir'awn (10:88). Ayat 94–97 run together as one movement: a doubt with a stated remedy (94), a prohibition against belying the signs of Allah, with loss as its outcome (95), and then a statement about people who will not believe even if every sign comes to them (96–97). Ma'arif ul Qur'an says of the last three that "the same subject finds support and emphasis while carrying a warning to those who are heedless."

## Ayah 94: an address to the Prophet ﷺ who is not the intended recipient

The verse opens with a condition — *fa-in kunta fī shakkin*, "if you are in doubt." The word for doubt here is *shakk*: an unsettled mind.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an is explicit about how to read this. The address is obviously to the Holy Prophet ﷺ, "but, it goes without saying that there is no probability of his doubting the revelation." So what is the address for? The commentary gives two possibilities.

**First**, the purpose is "to beam the message to the Muslim community through this address where he is not the intended recipient." The words land on the Prophet ﷺ and are meant for everyone listening — rather as a teacher will say something pointedly to the front row so that the whole room hears it.

**Second**, Ma'arif ul Qur'an adds that "it is also possible that this address may be to human beings at large," asking them whether they had any doubts about the Divine revelation sent to them through Sayyidna Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ. If they had, "let them ask those who recited the Torah and Injil before them."

And what would those readers say? According to Ma'arif ul Qur'an, "they would tell them that all past prophets and their Books have been announcing the glad tidings of the Last among Prophets. This will remove their scruples and suspicions."

## What the earlier scriptures were supposed to confirm

Ibn Kathir gives this section of his commentary a heading that sums up the argument: **Previous books attest to the truth of the Qur'an.** He anchors it in another verse:

> "Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet who can neither read nor write whom they find written of with them in the Tawrah and the Injil." (7:157)

The Prophet ﷺ who could neither read nor write is described, on this verse's testimony, in the scriptures already in their possession. Ibn Kathir then says something striking about the real state of their knowledge: "They are as certain of this as they are about who their children are, yet they hide it and distort it. They did not believe in it despite its clear evidence."

Note where that sentence sits in his commentary. It comes immediately before he quotes ayat 96–97, and he joins the two with a single connective: **"Therefore Allah said."** In his presentation, the verses about people who will not believe follow directly from the description of people who were certain, and who concealed and distorted what they were certain of.

## The verse answers its own condition

Ayah 94 does not leave the hypothetical dangling. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the rest of the verse: "Verily, the truth has come to you from your Lord. So be not of those who doubt (it)."

A doubt is entertained, a means of checking it is named — ask those who are reading the Book before you — and then the matter is closed with a declaration: *the truth has come to you from your Lord.*

## A practical ruling from ayah 94: take your doubts to people who know

Ma'arif ul Qur'an draws a rule of conduct from this verse, citing **Tafsir Mazhari**: "anyone in doubt about some religious matter is duty-bound to have his doubts removed by asking genuine ʿUlamāʾ" — meaning, as the commentary defines it, "religious scholars whose learning, honesty and adherence to Qur'an, and Sunnah is well recognized, popularly referred to as ʿUlamāʾ al-Haqq." And then the closing line: **"To continue nursing such doubts is not a good thing to do."**

This is worth sitting with, because of how it treats doubt. A doubt is met here with a prescribed remedy — an obligation to go and get it resolved. What the ruling faults is the nursing of it: keeping the question, unaddressed, indefinitely.

The definition of whom to ask is doing real work too. Three qualities are named together — **learning**, **honesty**, and **well-recognised adherence to the Qur'an and Sunnah**. The commentary requires them jointly; none of the three on its own is what the ruling asks you to look for. In an age when anyone with a platform can answer a religious question, that is a filter worth keeping.

## Ayah 95: the warning, and where it lands

"And do not be one of those who deny Allah's signs, or you will be one of the losers." Ibn Kathir renders it: "And be not one of those who belie the Ayat of Allah, for then you shall be one of the losers."

Two prohibitions stand back to back across the two verses in his rendering — *be not of those who doubt (it)*, at the close of 94, and *be not one of those who belie the Ayat of Allah*, in 95 — with the consequence named plainly: to be "one of the losers."

Ma'arif ul Qur'an tells us who this is for. Verses 95, 96 and 97 give "the same subject support and emphasis while carrying a warning to those who are heedless." The warning is aimed at the heedless listener.

## Ayat 96–97: denial that has hardened past reach

"Indeed, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe — even if every sign should come to them — until they see the painful torment."

**"The Word of your Lord has been justified against them."** The Arabic is *ḥaqqat ʿalayhim kalimatu rabbik*. Ibn Kathir's translation glosses *kalimat* here as "the Word (wrath) of your Lord." And in his commentary this verdict is not introduced in isolation: it follows straight on from his account of people who were as certain of the truth as they were of their own children, and hid it anyway.

**What "will not believe" means.** Ibn Kathir is careful here, because on its face the statement could seem contradicted by the end of ayah 97, where they do finally believe at the sight of the punishment. His explanation: "meaning they would not believe in a way that they might benefit from that belief. This is when they believe at a time one may not be able to benefit from his belief."

So the closing words of ayah 97 — *until they see the painful torment* — are not, on Ibn Kathir's reading, a promise of eventual faith that counts. They mark the point at which belief no longer brings the believer any benefit.

**Ibn Kathir's example: Fir'awn.** He names one directly — "An example is when Musa prayed against Fir'awn and his chiefs" — and quotes that prayer from earlier in this same surah:

> "Our Lord! Destroy their wealth, and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful torment." (10:88)

The same phrase — *until they see the painful torment* — stands in Musa's supplication and in ayah 97.

**And every possible sign.** Ibn Kathir then cites a second verse in the same passage:

> "And even if We had sent down unto them angels, and the dead had spoken unto them, and We had gathered together all things before their very eyes, they would not have believed, unless Allah willed, but most of them behave ignorantly." (6:111)

Angels descending, the dead speaking, everything gathered before their very eyes — and the verse says they would not have believed.

**A note on decree and responsibility.** The sources hold two things together here without collapsing either. On one side, the Word of Allah has been justified against them, and 6:111 says plainly "unless Allah willed" — this is affirmed exactly as it comes, without adding to it. On the other side, Ibn Kathir's account of these people is entirely about what they did: they were certain, they hid it and distorted it, and "did not believe in it despite its clear evidence." Allah's will and their own refusal both stand in the commentary; neither is presented as cancelling the other, and it is better to affirm both as the sources state them than to press further than they do.

## Living it

**Do not sit on a doubt.** The ruling from Tafsir Mazhari is the most directly actionable thing in this passage. If a religious question is unsettled in you, you are duty-bound to have it removed by asking someone with learning, honesty, and well-recognised adherence to the Qur'an and Sunnah — and not to go on nursing it.

**Take the remedy the commentary actually prescribes.** Ayah 94 offers a way of checking; ayah 95 warns against belying the signs of Allah, and names loss as the outcome; Ma'arif ul Qur'an says the warning is for the heedless. Acting on an unsettled question, rather than leaving it, is the response the commentary sets out.

**Do not read every refusal as a shortage of evidence.** On Ibn Kathir's account, the people in view had clear evidence and certainty, and hid it. And 6:111, which he cites here, describes people whom angels and the speaking dead would not have moved. When truth is refused, the commentary locates the cause in the refusers.

**Do not schedule your faith for later.** The most sobering line in the passage, on Ibn Kathir's reading, is that some people do eventually believe — at a time when one may not be able to benefit from his belief. Faith is worth something while it is still faith. That is now.

passages.title: Jonah's people, and faith only by Allah's leave
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** After the long account of Pharaoh — who said "I believe" only once the punishment had already seized him — these three ayat pose a question about the whole history of Allah's messengers: was there ever a town that came to faith *while faith still counted*? One town only: the people of Yunus (peace be upon him). The passage then turns straight to the Prophet ﷺ, and tells him that faith was never his to force out of anyone; it comes by Allah's leave. One thread runs through all three: **the timing of faith, and the giving of it.**

## The regret folded into the question

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the sense of the opening: *"So, how is it that there never was a town which could have believed and its belief would have been of benefit to it, except the people of Yunus (Jonah)!"* The tone, it says, is one of "regret over the state of inertia prevailing among common residents of habitations around the world" — and in that spirit the question is put: "How would they not become such as would have believed at a time when believing is acceptable and beneficial?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the heedless deniers of truth are being admonished "for their failure to make the optimum use of the time of life allowed to them. There was still time for them to leave denial and contumacy." Belief is of no use "at the hour of death, or the punishment, or after being neck deep in it, or at the time Doomsday sets in, for the doors of repentance will then be closed."

Both renderings hold two things together, not one: that a town *believed*, and that its belief *benefited* it. Ibn Kathir's rendering makes the same distinction — "Was there any town (community) that believed (after seeing the punishment), and its faith (at that moment) saved it (from the punishment)?"

## One town, in all that history

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as a question Allah poses: "did any town from the previous nations, believe in its entirety when they received the Messengers? All of the Messengers that We sent before you, O Muhammad, were denied by their people or the majority of their people." He gathers the Qur'an's own verdict: *"Alas for mankind! There never came a Messenger to them but they used to mock at him"* (36:30); *"no Messenger came to those before them but they said: 'A sorcerer or a madman!'"* (51:52); and the luxurious ones of every town answering, *"We found our fathers following a certain way and religion, and we will indeed follow their footsteps"* (43:23).

Then he cites what he describes as the authentic Hadith — our source names no collection for it — in which the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "The Prophets were displayed before me. There was a Prophet who passed with a group of people, and a Prophet who passed with only one man, a Prophet with two men, and a Prophet with no one."

Ibn Kathir's point is plain: between Musa and Yunus, peace be upon them, there was no nation that believed in its entirety except the people of Yunus, the people of Naynawā (Nineveh).

Why did they believe? Ibn Kathir is candid: "they only believed because they feared that the torment from which their Messenger warned them, might strike them. They actually witnessed its signs." Then: "So they cried to Allah and asked for help. They engaged in humility in invoking Him. They brought their children and cattle and asked Allah to lift the torment from which their Prophet had warned them. As a result, Allah sent His mercy and removed the scourge from them and gave them respite."

Qatadah's report, which Ibn Kathir preserves, adds: "When they lost their Prophet and they thought that the scourge was close upon them, **Allah sent through their hearts the desire to repent.** So they wore woolen fabrics and they separated each animal from its offspring. They then cried out to Allah for forty nights. When Allah saw the truth in their hearts and that they were sincere in their repentance and regrets, He removed the scourge from them." Qatadah locates them at Naynawā, the land of Mosul; the same is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others from the Salaf.

## The night the punishment was lifted

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the fuller account and is honest about its standing: the parts mentioned in the Qur'an, or proved from authentic narratives of Hadith, are certain; the rest comes from historical reports on which no ruling of Islamic law can be based.

Yunus (peace be upon him) was sent to the people of Nineveh, near Mosul — a people the Qur'an numbers at more than one hundred thousand. They refused to believe. Allah then commanded him to warn them that the punishment would overtake them within three days. He made the announcement and left.

The townspeople consulted one another, and what stopped them dismissing the warning was this: **they had never once found Yunus lying.** So they devised a test — watch whether he stays among them through the night. If he went elsewhere, they should be certain that ruin would descend the next morning. He moved out of his dwelling during the night, as he had been divinely commanded.

When morning came, the punishment appeared as a cloud-like black smoke hovering over their heads, tending downward, closer. They looked for their prophet, so that they could confess their denial, repent and believe with him as witness — and could not find him. They left their homes and came out onto open ground, women, children and animals huddled together, wearing rags, repenting and begging refuge, until the whole area resounded with one massive collective plaint. Allah accepted their repentance and removed the punishment. Reports indicate this was ʿĀshūrāʾ, the tenth of Muharram.

## Did they see the punishment, or only its signs?

The legal principle of the ayah rests on this. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Al-Qurtubi reporting three positions:

- **Ibn Jubayr:** the punishment had already covered them "like the sheet of cloth on the grave"; then, as their repentance turned out to be sound, Allah lifted it from them.
- **At-Tabari:** the people of Yunus were given a special place among all other peoples, in that their repentance was accepted *after* they had seen the punishment — a view mentioned by a large number of commentators.
- **Az-Zajjāj:** the punishment had not yet fallen on them. They had seen only the **signs** that proved it was coming. Had they seen the very punishment falling upon them, their believing would have been no good for them.

Al-Qurtubi judges Az-Zajjāj's statement the better one. The kind of seeing after which repentance is not accepted is the seeing "in which one is seized — as it happened in the case of Pharaoh." And that, he notes, is precisely why this Surah takes up the event of Yunus's people immediately after the event of Pharaoh: so that the difference becomes clear. Al-Qurtubi supports this with a saying of the Prophet ﷺ — again, no collection is named in our source — that "Allah Taʿālā accepts the Taubah of the servant until he is rattled by death," the *ghargharah* being the rattling sound from the throat of one being seized by death. He adds that the same sense is evident from the report of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, that Yunus's people had repented before the punishment actually fell. On this explanation, Al-Qurtubi concludes, "there remains no difficulty, or contradiction, or particularization."

**Where the scholars genuinely differ, hold both with respect.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to record that even those who called it special never said the reason was any shortcoming on the part of Yunus (peace be upon him). The reasons they gave were the honest repentance of those people and their sincere belief.

## Where the door of repentance actually closes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the rule: **the door of repentance does not close even when a worldly punishment comes face to face.** It closes when the punishment of the Hereafter comes face to face — which means either the Day of Qiyāmah, or the moment of death, "whether it is natural death or death as a victim of some worldly punishment as was the case with the Pharaoh."

So the acceptance of the repentance of Yunus's people is not contrary to the divine law; it falls under it: they repented when they saw the punishment coming, but certainly before it overtook them, and before death. Pharaoh and others repented only after the punishment had overtaken them, at the time of the last rattle of death — "therefore, their believing was not valid and trustworthy and the Taubah they made was not accepted."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precedent from the Qur'an itself: Banī Isrāʾīl, with the Mount of Ṭūr left dangling above them so that they were scared enough to repent — *"And raised high above you the Mount: 'Hold fast to what We have given to you'"* (2:63). They repented before the punishment materialised and before death overtook them, simply on noticing the imminent danger; and their repentance was accepted. Same rule, different nation.

## A necessary defence of Yunus, peace be upon him

Some contemporaries had made what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls a grave error — it quotes *Tafhīm al-Qurʼān* of Maulana Mawdudi — attributing to Yunus (peace be upon him) shortcomings in the discharge of his duties as a prophet: that he became impatient and abandoned his station before time, and that Allah therefore could not in justice punish a people against whom the argument had not been conclusively established.

The reply begins from a settled point of creed: **the prophets, peace be upon them all, are protected from sins — maʿṣūm.** This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is an uncontested belief on which there is consensus of the Muslim Ummah. Partial differences do exist in the details — whether the protection covers minor sins as well as major ones, whether it includes the period before prophethood — but no difference exists among any individuals or groups on this: that the blessed prophets can never fall short in carrying out their duty as prophets. "If a prophet does not stand protected even from this short-coming, then, there is no use for protection from other sins."

On the facts: there is no Qur'anic hint that Yunus broke away from his people without prior divine permission. The pattern with past communities — clearly mentioned in the Qur'an in connection with Lut — is that when the decision was made to send punishment, Allah would command His Messenger to leave that area. So his departure, after delivering the three-day warning, obviously took place under divine orders.

**What, then, was the slip?** When the punishment did not materialise, returning meant being charged as a liar, and the law of that people required that a proven liar be killed. Prophets, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reminds us, are protected from every act of sin and disobedience "but are not set apart from others in terms of human nature and temperament." So he set out to migrate. The slip "was no more than that he boarded a boat with the intention of migration, before came the permission of Allah" — in itself no sin.

The Qur'an's own wording carries this. In 37:140: *idh abaqa ilā al-fulk al-mashḥūn* — "when he ran away towards the laden boat." The word *abaqa* denotes displeasure, and means the running away or fleeing of a slave without the permission of his master. In 21:87: *"and the man of the fish, when he left in anger assuming that We shall not keep him tight"* — displeasure over an act of migration prompted by natural apprehension and the desire to stay safe from a hostile people. And all of this happened *after* the perfect fulfilment of the duties of prophethood, when returning posed a certain danger to his life. Tafsir Ruh al-Maʿānī says the same: he left his people in anger at their bitter hostility and adamant refusal "despite that he had spent a long time as a prophet inviting them to faith… This journey of his was a kind of migration but he had not yet received the permission for it."

The accusation can only stand on **Isrāʾīliyyāt** — reports transmitted from earlier scriptural traditions, which commentators generally do include in their tafsirs, but about which all of them agree that they are not authentic and trustworthy, and on which no Islamic legal ruling can be based. "No commentator of Islam has ever approved of it."

## What happened at sea

The rest belongs to that same class of historical report. Yunus (peace be upon him) waited outside the township, knowing nothing of their repentance, anxious about being declared a liar. He reached the shore, where people recognised him and let him board a boat without charge. Offshore the boat stopped dead, and the boatmen announced that their boat was made such that it halts when an oppressive sinner or a slave in flight boards it.

Yunus spoke out that he was the one, and asked to be thrown into the sea so that others would not suffer. They refused, and drew lots; his name came up, again and again — *"and he drew lots and was among the losers"* (37:141). A large fish waited under divine orders, commanded that the body deposited in her belly was no food for her but his home for a while. Ibn Masʿūd said he remained forty days; the period is also reported as five, and as a day and a few hours (Mazhari) — "Only Allah knows the truth about it."

What is certain is the duʿāʾ the Qur'an preserves: *lā ilāha illā anta subḥānaka innī kuntu min al-ẓālimīn* — "There is no god but You. Pure are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers" (21:87). Allah accepted this prayer, and he was put on the shore alive and unharmed: the heat had left no hair on his body, so Allah caused a gourd vine to grow near him for shade, and a wild goat would come morning and evening so that he had milk to drink. Thus he was alerted to that slip.

## The turn to the Prophet ﷺ: what a messenger cannot do

Ibn Kathir gives the meaning of *"And had your Lord willed"*: "O Muhammad, if it had been the will of your Lord, He would make all the people of the earth believe in what you have brought to them. **But Allah has wisdom in what He does.**" He lines this up with 11:118–119 — Allah could surely have made mankind one Ummah, but they will not cease to disagree — and with 13:31, "had Allah willed, He could have guided all mankind."

Then the question: *"So, will you then compel mankind… until they become believers?"* Ibn Kathir's gloss: "it is not for you to do that. You are not commanded to do that either." Guidance belongs to the One who "sends astray whom He wills, and guides whom He wills" (35:8).

What follows in Ibn Kathir is a chain of verses in which Allah lifts the weight off His Prophet's ﷺ shoulders: *"So do not destroy yourself in sorrow for them"*; *"It is not up to you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills"* (2:272); *"It may be that you would kill yourself with grief because they are not believers"* (26:3); *"you guide not who you like"* (28:56); *"Your duty is only to convey, and it is up to Us to reckon"* (13:40); *"So remind, you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them"* (88:21–22). These ayat, he says, prove that Allah is the doer of what He wants, guiding whom He wills, leading whom He wills to stray — and then comes the qualification that must never be dropped: **"all out of His knowledge, wisdom, and justice."**

## "Except by the leave of Allah"

*"It is not for any person to believe, except by the leave of Allah"* — *bi-idhnillāh*. Ibn Kathir places this ayah as the summation of everything above, in the same breath as that qualification.

The second half is severe: *"and He will put the Rijs on those who do not reason."* Ibn Kathir explains *rijs* here as **disorder and misguidance**, and takes "those who do not reason" to be about Allah's proofs and evidences. He closes: "He is the Just in all matters, guiding whom He wills to guide, and leading whom He wills astray."

## Living it

**Faith has a clock on it.** That is not a threat but a mercy, because the clock is still running — exactly the admonition Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out: they still had the time; they could put their obstinacy aside and believe as the people of Yunus did.

**Sincerity is what was weighed.** Qatadah's line: "When Allah saw the truth in their hearts and that they were sincere in their repentance and regrets, He removed the scourge from them." They could not even find their prophet to stand as witness. They went out in rags and wept, and it was enough.

**Fear can be a legitimate door.** Ibn Kathir says plainly that they believed because they feared the torment they had been warned of — and Allah answered them, removed the scourge, and "permitted them to enjoy for a while." Do not despise a repentance that begins in fear.

**And the desire to repent was itself sent.** Qatadah's wording: "Allah sent through their hearts the desire to repent." That sits perfectly beside the last ayah — no soul believes except by the leave of Allah. If you have any inclination toward Him at all, that inclination was a gift before it was a decision.

**For anyone carrying the weight of someone else's guidance** — a parent, a teacher, anyone lying awake over a person they love who will not turn — these last two ayat lift exactly that weight, and Ibn Kathir shows them lifting it first from the Prophet ﷺ, who felt it more than we do. Convey, remind, pray, and leave the outcome where it has always belonged.

passages.title: Signs that do not persuade; messengers delivered
passages.tafsir:
Ayah 101 opens with a command — behold all that is in the heavens and the earth — and then states plainly that neither the signs nor the warners benefit a people who will not believe. Ayah 102 asks such people what they are waiting for, if not the like of the days of those who passed away before them, and instructs the Prophet ﷺ to answer: wait, then; I am waiting with you. Ayah 103 gives the outcome: We save Our messengers and those who believed, and it is binding upon Us to save the believers.

Ibn Kathir comments on all three as one continuous passage.

## "Behold all that is in the heavens and the earth"

Ibn Kathir reads the opening command as Allah guiding His servants to reflect upon His blessings: what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth is part of the clear signs **for those who possess correct understanding**. That last qualification carries the weight of the whole passage — the signs are public, the understanding is not.

From the heavens: the luminous stars, the firmaments, the moving planetary bodies, the sun and the moon; the night and the day, their alternating and their merging, so that one grows long and the other short, then they alternate through the year so the long becomes short and the short becomes long. The rising of the sun, its vastness, its beauty, its adornment. The rain Allah sends down from the heavens, bringing the earth to life after its death and causing fruits, crops, flowers and plants to grow.

And from the earth: the various species of beasts, with their differing colours and their benefits for man. The mountains, the plains, the deserts, the civilisations, the structures, the barren lands. Then the wonders of the sea and its waves — and yet, for all that, it has been made subservient and submissive to those who travel upon its surface, carrying their ships so they traverse it with ease.

Ibn Kathir's conclusion is the point of the whole list: **all of this is under the control of the Most Able; there is none worthy of worship except Him, and there is no true Lord other than Him.**

## Why signs and warners can fail to move a person

The second half of ayah 101 — *wa mā tughnī al-āyāt wa'l-nudhur ʿan qawmin lā yuʾminūn* — is usually rendered as a flat statement: neither the signs nor the warners benefit those who do not believe. Ibn Kathir voices it as a question with a sting in it: *what thing will benefit such disbelieving people besides the heavenly and earthly signs, and the Messengers with their miracles, proofs and evidences that clearly prove the truthfulness of their message?*

Note the pairing: *al-āyāt* (the signs) and *al-nudhur* (the warners). On Ibn Kathir's gloss these are the heavenly and earthly signs on one side, and the messengers with their miracles and proofs on the other — the silent testimony of creation and the spoken testimony of the messengers. This passage closes both doors at once for a certain kind of person.

Ibn Kathir grounds this in the surah itself, citing ayah 96: *Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe.* The failure is not in the evidence. Something has settled in them that evidence no longer reaches.

## "Then what are they waiting for?"

Ayah 102 shifts to the consequence. *Fahal yantaẓirūna illā mithla ayyāmi'lladhīna khalaw min qablihim* — "Then do they wait save for the likes of the days of men who passed away before them?" Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: are these who reject you, Muhammad ﷺ, waiting for the vengeance and torment like **the Days of Allah**, when He punished those who came before them of the previous nations that rejected their messengers?

Then comes the reply the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to give: *Say: "Wait then, I am waiting with you among those who wait."* He is not told to argue further, and he is not told to threaten. He simply agrees to wait — and the next ayah says what the waiting produces.

## The pattern that never fails

Ibn Kathir joins the end of 102 to 103 as one statement. *Thumma nunajjī rusulanā wa'lladhīna āmanū* — "Then We save Our Messengers and those who believe!" — carries, he says, the meaning: **verily, We destroy those who reject the messengers.** The destruction is not stated outright in these words; Ibn Kathir reads it as what they imply. The verse names who is brought out, and by that names what happened to the rest.

Then the closing phrase: *kadhālika ḥaqqan ʿalaynā nunji'l-muʾminīn* — "Thus it is incumbent upon Us to save the believers." Ibn Kathir explains that this is **a right that Allah, the Exalted, has obligated upon His Noble Self**, and he places it beside 6:54: *Your Lord has written (prescribed) mercy for Himself.*

Nothing outside Allah imposes anything on Him; no creature holds a claim over its Creator. What these two verses report is that Allah has bound Himself, out of His own mercy. So the believer's security does not rest on his own worth or leverage. It rests on a pledge Allah made about Himself — which is a far stronger place to stand.

Notice also that in ayah 103 the rescue is not confined to the messengers: it is *rusulanā wa'lladhīna āmanū*, "Our Messengers and those who believe." The ordinary believer is inside the same guarantee as the prophet he followed.

## The town whose belief came in time: Nineveh

Just a few ayat earlier, in 10:98, this surah asked: *So, how is it that there never was a town which could have believed and its belief would have been of benefit to it, except the people of Yunus!* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out that event, drawing on what the Qur'an mentions along with reports of hadith and of history.

The people of Yunus (peace be upon him) lived at the well-known place, Nineveh, near Mosul in Iraq, and the Qur'an gives their number as more than one hundred thousand. Allah sent Yunus (peace be upon him) for their guidance; they refused to believe; and Allah asked him to warn them that the punishment would overtake them within three days. He made the announcement before his people and left. His people conferred among themselves and agreed on a telling thing: **they had never found him lying**, so this thing from him was not to be ignored. They devised a plan — if he stayed among them at his place through the night, they were to understand that nothing would happen; and if he went elsewhere, they should be certain the punishment would descend the next morning. He moved out of his dwelling place during the night, as he had been divinely commanded.

When morning came, the punishment appeared as a cloud-like black smoke hovering over their heads and tending to descend closer to them. They became certain they were all going to be destroyed. They looked for Yunus (peace be upon him), so that they could confess their past denial, repent and believe with him as their witness — and could not find him. So they took it upon themselves to repent and seek forgiveness with the best sincerity at their command. They left their homes and came out onto open ground, women, children and animals all huddled together, wearing rags, weeping and wailing, repenting and begging refuge from the punishment, until the whole area resounded with one massive collective plea. Allah accepted their repentance and removed the punishment from them. Reports indicate this was ʿĀshūrā, the tenth of Muharram.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an honest caveat: whatever parts of this story are mentioned in the Qur'an, or stand proved from authentic narratives of hadith, are certain; the rest come from historical reports, and no ruling of Islamic law can be based on them.

## How long the door stays open

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the principle out precisely: **the door of repentance does not close even when a worldly punishment comes face to face** — but repentance is not accepted at the time the punishment of the Hereafter comes face to face, which means either the Day of Qiyamah or the time of death, whether natural death or death as a victim of some worldly punishment, as was the case with Pharaoh.

So the people of Yunus were no breach of the divine law; their case falls squarely under it. They made their repentance when they saw the punishment coming, but they did so *before* it overtook them, and before death. Pharaoh did the opposite — he said he believed only after the punishment had already overtaken him, at the time of the last rattle of death, and his believing was not accepted.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a precedent from within the Qur'an itself: the Children of Israel, over whose heads the mount of Tur was raised — *And raised high above you the Mount of Tur: "Hold fast to what We have given to you"* (2:63) — repented when they saw the danger, and their repentance was accepted, because they repented well before any punishment materialised and before death overtook them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most commentators — Abu Hayyan, al-Qurtubi, al-Zamakhshari, Qadi Thanaullah, ʿAllamah Alusi and others — read the ayah this way, so that the acceptance of the Ninevites' repentance comes under the customary divine law. It also reports, in al-Qurtubi's words, where earlier authorities differed:

- **Ibn Jubayr:** the punishment had covered them up like the sheet of cloth on a grave; then, as their repentance turned out to be sound, Allah lifted the punishment from them.
- **At-Tabari:** the people of Yunus were given a special place among all other peoples, in that their repentance was accepted *after* they had seen the punishment — a view mentioned by a large number of commentators.
- **Az-Zajjaj:** the punishment had not yet fallen on them at all; they had only seen the signs that proved its coming. Had they seen the very punishment falling upon them, their believing would have been no good to them.

Al-Qurtubi judged az-Zajjaj's statement the better one, reasoning that the "seeing" after which repentance is not accepted means the seeing in which one is *seized* by the punishment, as in the case of Pharaoh — and that this is why, in this very surah, the event of the people of Yunus was taken up immediately after the event of Pharaoh, so the difference would be clear. He supports it with a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that Allah accepts the repentance of a servant until he is rattled by death; *al-ghargharah* is the rattling sound that comes from the throat, and that is the state of being seized by death. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this through al-Qurtubi without naming a collection.) The same sense is evident, al-Qurtubi says, from the narration of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, in which the people of Yunus repented before the punishment actually fell. On this explanation, he concludes, there remains no difficulty, no contradiction, and no need to treat the people of Yunus as a special exception.

Read together, Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān give ayah 102 its full weight. The "days" of the earlier nations are real; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's comment on 10:98 is that the heedless deniers were admonished precisely for failing to make the best use of the time of life allowed to them, when there was still time to leave denial behind.

## Defending the honour of Yunus (peace be upon him)

Having established that the removal of the punishment from the people of Yunus (peace be upon him) was not against the divine law but exactly in accordance with it, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns to what it calls a grave error made by some contemporaries: they attribute shortcomings to Yunus (peace be upon him) in the discharge of his duties as a prophet, and make that failing the cause both of the punishment being lifted from his people and of the divine displeasure mentioned in Surah al-Anbiya' and Surah as-Saffat. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the passage it is answering from Tafhim al-Qur'an by Maulana Mawdudi.)

Its answer rests first on a point of creed: the prophets, peace be upon them all, are *maʿsūm* — protected from sins. This is an uncontested belief on which there is a consensus of the Muslim Ummah. In its details some partial differences do exist — whether the protection covers minor sins as well as major ones, and whether it extends to the period before prophethood — but no individual or group differs on the belief that the prophets **can never fall short in carrying out their duty as prophets**. The reason given is that there could be no greater sin for a prophet than falling short in the very mission for which Allah chose him; if a prophet were not protected even from that, there would be no use in protection from anything else.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then answers the charge on its own ground. It says there is no Qur'anic hint that Yunus (peace be upon him) broke away from his people without divine permission after delivering the warning. On the contrary, the context of the verses and the reports from tafsir show that things happened here as they had with past communities: when the decision was made to send punishment on a people, Allah would command His messenger and his companions to leave that area — as is clearly mentioned in the Qur'an in connection with the story of Lut (peace be upon him). So his departure from Nineveh, after conveying that the punishment would come in three days, obviously took place under divine orders.

What, then, of the words of displeasure in 21:87–88 and 37:139–148? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains them not as a failure in the mission — which had been perfectly fulfilled — but as a *slip* measured against the elegant prophetic station he was blessed with. After the punishment did not materialise, Yunus (peace be upon him) was worried about returning to his people: they would charge him with lying, and the law of those people required that a proven liar be killed. Under those circumstances he had no way out but to migrate. But the customary practice of the prophets is that they do not migrate on their own opinion, without a signal from Allah. So the slip was no more than that he boarded a boat intending migration before the permission of Allah came — in itself no sin, but contrary to the customary practice of prophets, and therefore received with displeasure. This is why 37:140 says *idh abaqa ila'l-fulki'l-mashḥūn* ("when he ran away towards the laden boat"), using *abaqa*, a word for a slave running away without his master's permission; and why 21:87 speaks of him leaving *mughāḍiban*, in anger. Tafsir Ruh al-Maʿani puts it the same way: this journey of his was a kind of migration, but he had not yet received the permission for it.

Finally, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out where the accusation actually comes from. When the objection was pressed, the commentators cited in its support prove nothing of the kind — with the exception of some Israelite reports of Wahb ibn Munabbih and others. Commentators do generally include Israelite reports in their tafsirs, but all agree these are not authentic or trustworthy and no Islamic legal ruling can be based on them. It is only on those crutches, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that such a charge can be levelled at Yunus (peace be upon him), and no commentator of Islam has ever approved of it.

One further note it makes is worth carrying away: the noble prophets are protected from every act of sin and disobedience, but they are not set apart from others in human nature and temperament. Yunus (peace be upon him) naturally grieved — he had made the announcement exactly as commanded, and now that very announcement threatened to have him declared a liar.

## Living it

**Look on purpose.** Ibn Kathir's inventory is an instruction, not decoration. Take one item from it this week — the shortening and lengthening of the day, rain on dead ground, a ship the sea carries with ease — and follow it all the way to his conclusion: there is no true Lord other than Him. The signs are useless as scenery and decisive as evidence; the difference is in the looking.

**Stop auditing the evidence.** Ayah 101 describes a person for whom more proof changes nothing. If the heavens, the earth and a messenger are already on the table, the shortage was never in the evidence.

**Do not spend the interval.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's charge against the deniers in 10:98 is that they were not making the best use of the time still allowed to them. Repentance is accepted right up to the death-rattle — but no one is told when that arrives. Delay is a wager on information you do not have.

**Repent openly and together.** Nineveh's model was not private regret. They came out onto open ground, whole families and even their animals, in rags, weeping and begging refuge — a whole town pleading at once. Allah accepted their repentance and removed the punishment from them.

**And take ayah 103 to heart when you are outnumbered.** Allah has made the rescue of the believers a right upon His own Noble Self. Whatever the deniers are waiting for, the believer is waiting for something else — and his waiting rests on a pledge Allah made about Himself.

passages.title: The Prophet's declaration of his own religion
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are one dictated speech. Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ exactly what to say to people who are in doubt about the religion he brought — and what he is told to say is not so much an argument as a declaration: *this* is what I worship, *this* is what I will not worship, and *this* is why. Ayah 104 gives the refusal; ayah 105 gives the positive command that belongs with it; ayah 106 forbids invoking anything besides Allah; ayah 107 supplies the ground the whole passage stands on — that harm and good are in one Hand alone. Ibn Kathir gathers all four under a single heading: **"The Command to worship Allah Alone and rely upon Him."**

## "Say: O mankind"

The passage opens with **qul** — "Say" — so every word that follows is dictated. The Prophet ﷺ is not composing a position; he is delivering one.

And the address is wide: *yā ayyuhā an-nās*, which Ibn Kathir renders "O mankind." Not "O Quraysh," not "O you who reject" — the declaration is put to human beings as such, and it still is.

What follows is a reply to **doubt**. Ibn Kathir spells out what the doubt was about: "If you are in doubt about the correctness of that which I have been sent with — the *Hanif* religion, the religion which Allah has revealed to me." Notice that the answer given to doubt is not a chain of proofs but a life. Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah reads: **"I will never worship those whom you worship besides Allah, rather, I will worship Allah, the One Who cause you to die."** His explanation states the same thing plainly: **"I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah. Rather, I worship Allah alone, ascribing no partners to Him."** A settled position, stated without hedging.

Ibn Kathir then presses the point to its sharpest edge — a hypothetical the Prophet ﷺ concedes for argument's sake and still refuses: *"If the gods that you call upon are real, I still refuse to worship them. So call upon them and ask them to harm me, and you will see that they can bring no harm or benefit. The only One Who holds the power of harm and benefit in His Hand is Allah alone, Who has no partners."*

## "The One Who causes you to die"

Of every name and description that could have been chosen here, ayah 104 identifies Allah as **the One Who causes you to die**. Ibn Kathir opens it out: "He is the One Who causes you to die just as He gives you life. Then, unto Him is your final return."

Think about who is being addressed. These are people in doubt about the religion the Prophet ﷺ brought, confident enough in their own gods to stay where they are. And the description slipped into his reply reaches past the argument and touches the one fact none of them can arrange, delay, or delegate. The gods they call upon, Ibn Kathir says, "can bring no harm or benefit" — but the One he worships gives life, takes it, and receives the return. The whole dispute is being placed in front of the moment when it will be settled.

## "And I was commanded"

Ayah 104 closes with **"And I was commanded to be one of the believers"** — the language of a servant under orders. Even the Prophet's ﷺ own faith is presented as something he was *commanded* into. The message he carries binds him first.

Ibn Kathir's rendering of ayah 105 then continues in the same voice, supplying words in brackets to show it: **"And (I was commanded), 'Direct your face toward the Hanif religion, and not be one of the idolators.'"** And when he reaches that last prohibition — **"and not be one of the idolators"** — he notes that it is **"directly connected with the previous statement, *And I was commanded to be one of the believers*."** The refusal of idolatry is not a separate topic that happens to follow; Ibn Kathir ties it straight back to the command the Prophet ﷺ was given in the ayah before.

## Setting the face: what *ḥanīf* means

Ibn Kathir's rendering of ayah 105 reads: **"Direct your face toward the *Hanif* religion."** Our translation renders the sense as "be steadfast in faith in all uprightness." The image is a bodily one — the face is the part of a person that shows which way he is going.

But Ibn Kathir takes it inward. Directing the face toward the religion, he says, "means to make one's intention in worship solely for Allah alone, being a *Hanif*." The outward posture is a picture of the inward one: intention aimed at Allah with nothing else in the aim.

And he gives us a precise definition of the key word: **"*Hanif* means one who turns away from associating partners with Allah."** It is not a vague piety and not a neutral middle position. It is a *turning away* — a deliberate movement of the whole self off one road and onto another. That is exactly why, Ibn Kathir notes, Allah immediately adds the other half: **"and not be one of the idolators."** As he puts it, "For this reason Allah says" it. The positive and the negative are one instruction stated twice.

Two ways of saying one thing, then: aim everything at Allah, and belong to no one else's aim.

## "Do not invoke what cannot benefit or harm you"

Ayah 106 narrows from worship in general to one act in particular: calling upon, invoking. Ibn Kathir's rendering: **"And do not invoke besides Allah what will not benefit you nor harm you. For if you did, you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers."**

The reasoning is deliberately unflattering to the idols. They are not attacked as ugly or foreign or new. They are dismissed on the only ground that matters when you are actually in need: **they cannot do anything to you.** They cannot deliver a benefit; they cannot even manage a harm. A being that can neither help nor hurt is, whatever else it is, not worth calling. Ibn Kathir's invitation stands: call them, and ask them to harm me.

And there is a quiet resonance in the word chosen for the outcome — **wrongdoers**. This is the surah in which the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, and his people is told, and Ma'ariful-Qur'an quotes the du'a he made in the belly of the fish, from 21:87: *"There is no god but You. Pure are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers."* Allah accepted that prayer, our source says, and he "was put on the shore alive and unharmed." The word ayah 106 warns a person not to fall into is the word Yunus used of himself in his plea. It is a category one escapes by confessing it.

## Ayah 107: the reason under everything

Ayah 107 is where the passage's argument is finally laid bare: **"And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none who can lift it but He. And if He intends good for you, then none can repel His favour, which He causes to reach whom He wills among His servants."**

Ibn Kathir's comment is short and decisive: "This verse contains the explanation that good, evil, benefit and harm only come from Allah alone and no one shares with His power over these things. **Therefore, He is the One Who deserves to be worshipped alone, without ascription of partners.**" That "therefore" is the spine of all four ayat. Worship is not owed to whatever is old, or popular, or ancestral. It is owed to whoever actually holds harm and good — and that is One.

Feel the wording. Harm **touches** you — and against that touch there is **no one who can lift it but He**. On the other side, good is what He **intends** for you, and none can **repel** it — no one can intercept the favour on its way to the servant He wills it to reach.

This is why Ibn Kathir's heading for the passage is not only "worship Allah alone" but "**and rely upon Him**." Once you know that one power stands behind both the harm and the relief, there is nothing else left to appeal to. Nothing reaches you except from Him, and nothing He sends can be blocked on the way.

## The surah's own illustration

Ayah 107 was not an abstraction to the first listeners, because this surah had already shown it happening. Ma'ariful-Qur'an, commenting on the earlier part of the surah, recounts what our sources report about the people of Yunus, peace be upon him — the people of Nineveh, near Mosul in Iraq, more than a hundred thousand of them by the Qur'an's own reckoning.

They refused to believe. Yunus was told by Allah to warn them that the punishment would overtake them within three days, and he announced it. When morning came, Ma'ariful-Qur'an says, the punishment appeared "in the form of a cloud-like black smoke," hovering over their heads and tending to descend closer to them, and they became certain they were all going to be destroyed. They looked for Yunus so that they could confess, repent and believe with him as witness, and could not find him. So they did it themselves: they left their homes and came out on open ground — "women, children and animals all huddled there. Wearing rags, weeping and wailing, repenting and begging refuge from Divine punishment, they made the whole area resound with a massive collective plaint." And Allah accepted their repentance and removed the punishment from them.

That is ayah 107 in narrative form. The harm had already been announced and its sign was over their heads, and there was nothing in Nineveh that could lift it. **There is none who can lift it but He.** So they went, all of them, straight to Him.

Ma'ariful-Qur'an also cites a precedent from the Qur'an itself, on Qurtubi's authority: Bani Isra'il, with the mount of Tur raised over their heads until they were frightened into repentance — "And raised high above you the Mount of Tur: 'Hold fast to what We have given to you'" (2:63). They too repented on seeing the danger, before the punishment materialised, and their repentance was accepted.

The classical commentators differed over exactly how far the punishment had come. Ma'ariful-Qur'an cites al-Qurtubi reporting several views: Ibn Jubayr said the punishment had already covered them "like the sheet of cloth on the grave," and it was lifted when their repentance proved sound; at-Tabari held that the people of Yunus were given a special place among all other peoples, in that their repentance was accepted *after* they had seen the punishment, and this, he notes, has been mentioned by a large number of commentators; az-Zajjaj held that the punishment had not fallen on them at all — they had only seen the signs that proved it was coming — and that had they seen the punishment itself falling upon them, their believing would have been no good to them. Al-Qurtubi judged az-Zajjaj's view the better one, since the "seeing" after which repentance is no longer accepted means the one in which a person is *seized* by the punishment, as happened with Pharaoh — and it is telling, he notes, that this very surah takes up the story of Yunus's people immediately after the story of Pharaoh, so that the difference becomes clear. A narration from Sayyidna 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud is cited to the same effect: they repented before the punishment actually fell.

Ma'ariful-Qur'an is careful about the rest of the details, and the caution is worth carrying: what is in the Qur'an or stands proved from authentic narratives of Hadith is certain; the rest comes from historical reports, and no ruling of Islamic law can be based on them.

## A caution the commentary insists on

Ma'ariful-Qur'an devotes a long, deliberate passage to a claim it considers a grave error — that Yunus, peace be upon him, fell short in performing his duty as a prophet, and that this was somehow why the punishment was lifted from his people. It quotes the claim from *Tafhimul-Qur'an* by Maulana Mawdudi, and answers it at length.

Its first answer is a matter of belief: "the prophets, peace be upon them all, are protected from sins (*ma'sum*)" — divinely protected — and this, it says, "is an uncontested belief on which there is a consensus of the Muslim Ummah." It is honest about where scholars have differed in the details: whether this protection ('*ismah*) covers all kinds of minor sins or only the major ones, and whether it covers the period before a man is made a prophet. But on one point, it says, "no difference exists among any individuals or groups": that the prophets, all of them, can never fall short in carrying out their duty as prophets. There could be no greater failing for a prophet than neglecting the very mission he was chosen for.

Its second answer is that the premise is not needed in the first place. On Ma'ariful-Qur'an's reading — and it names Abu Hayyan, al-Qurtubi, al-Zamakhshari, Qadi Thana'ullah and 'Allamah Alusi among those who read the verse this way — the acceptance of Nineveh's repentance broke no Divine law at all but fell squarely within it, because they repented *before* the punishment seized them. And it observes that even at-Tabari and the others who did treat the event as exceptional never gave "shortcomings" of Yunus as the reason; they pointed instead to the honesty of the people's repentance.

What, then, of the words of displeasure in Surah al-Anbiya' (21:87–88) and Surah as-Saffat (37:139–148)? Ma'ariful-Qur'an says the slip was of a different kind entirely: he set out to migrate before the permission of Allah had come — "though no sin in itself," but contrary to the customary practice of the prophets. It quotes Tafsir Ruh al-Ma'ani: "This journey of his was a kind of migration but he had not yet received the permission for it." And it warns that the heavier accusation can only be propped up on Israelite reports, about which the commentators agree "that these are not authentic and trustworthy."

It closes that discussion with a prayer worth borrowing: "And Allah, He is Pure and High and the Most Knowledgeable, and before Him is our plaint that He protects us from all errors and lapses."

## "And He is the Pardoning, the Merciful"

Then the passage ends — and where it ends is astonishing.

A surah's worth of warning to the heedless deniers of truth; a Prophet ﷺ told to declare his separation from the idolaters in the plainest words available; a warning that even he would be among the wrongdoers if he invoked another. And the final word is: **al-Ghafūr, ar-Raḥīm** — the Pardoning, the Merciful.

Ibn Kathir does not soften it and does not let it be misread: "This means that He is forgiving and merciful towards those who turn to Him in repentance, **regardless of what sin the person has committed. Even if the person associated a partner with Allah, verily Allah would forgive him if he repented from it.**"

So the door is not being shut on the idolaters at the end of the surah. It is being held open. The declaration of ayah 104 — *I will never worship what you worship* — is a separation from the worship, not a sentence passed on the worshipper. He can walk through the door tonight.

How long does the door stay open? Ma'ariful-Qur'an, drawing on the earlier passage of this surah, draws the line carefully: "the door of Taubah does not close even when the worldly punishment comes face to face" — that is exactly what happened at Nineveh — but repentance "is not accepted at the time the punishment of the Hereafter comes face to face," which is either on the day of Qiyamah or at the time of death, whether that death is natural or comes as a worldly punishment, as it did to Pharaoh. Pharaoh and those like him, it says, repented only after the punishment had overtaken them, "at the time of the last rattle of death" — and so their believing was not valid and their repentance was not accepted. Al-Qurtubi supports the distinction with a saying of the Prophet ﷺ — quoted in our source without naming a collection — that Allah accepts the repentance of a servant until he is rattled by death; and *al-ghargharah*, al-Qurtubi explains, is the rattling sound that comes from the throat, which is what happens on being seized by death.

## Living it

- **When your religion is questioned, answer the way you were taught to here.** Not with anxiety and not with contempt: with a clear statement of what you worship and what you refuse, and a calm invitation to look at what the alternatives can actually do.
- **Aim the face.** Ibn Kathir reads "direct your face toward the religion" as intention — so the passage's demand lands on the inside of your worship. Where is this prayer, this charity, this effort actually pointed?
- **Watch what you call on when you are desperate.** Ayah 106's test is not theological sophistication but simple realism: can this thing benefit or harm me? Everything answers no except One.
- **Take both the harm and the relief from the One who sends them.** Ayah 107 forbids two panics at once: the panic that says *nothing can help me*, and the panic that says *someone can block what Allah is sending me*. Neither is true.
- **Do not conclude that you are past forgiving.** Ibn Kathir's comment on the last words of the passage is explicit — no sin, not even ascribing a partner to Allah, survives sincere repentance. And Nineveh repented with the smoke already over their heads.

passages.title: The truth has come: choose, follow, be patient
passages.tafsir:
**Sūrah Yūnus closes with an announcement and an instruction.** Ayah 108 is addressed outward, to everyone: the truth has come from your Lord, and whatever you do with it lands on your own account — and the Messenger ﷺ is not the one placed in charge of your believing. Ayah 109 turns inward, to the Prophet ﷺ alone: hold to what is revealed to you, bear the hostility, and wait for Allah's verdict.
