What binds the two ayat into one passage is a single division of responsibility. **The Messenger ﷺ delivers. The hearer chooses. Allah judges.** Once those three are in their proper places, nothing is left for the Messenger ﷺ to do except the two things ayah 109 names — follow, and be patient.

## Ayah 108: "The truth has surely come to you from your Lord"

Ibn Kathir opens with the point the whole ayah rests on: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to inform the people that what he has brought them from Allah **is the truth** — in Ibn Kathir's words, "a message concerning which there is no doubt or suspicion."

Three things in the wording repay attention.

**The address is to humanity.** The Prophet ﷺ is told to say *yā ayyuhā al-nās* — "O humanity!" Ibn Kathir renders it "O people!" and describes the command as one to inform *the people*. The claim being made is put to human beings as such.

**The truth is *min rabbikum*, "from your Lord."** The Prophet ﷺ is not the author of what he announces. Ibn Kathir's phrasing is careful on this: it is "that which he has brought them **from Allah**." The messenger carries it; the sender is their Lord.

**"Has surely come."** The ayah does not present the truth as something still on its way or still pending. It announces an arrival that has already happened. Everything that follows in the ayah is about what people now do with something that has already reached them.

## "Whoever is guided… whoever goes astray"

Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact: "whoever is guided by it **and follows it**, then he only benefits himself by doing so. Likewise, whoever is misguided away from this message, then he will suffer the consequences against his own self."

Notice that Ibn Kathir will not let guidance be a purely mental event. He joins two things — being guided *by* the message and *following* it. Recognising that something is true and then living as though it were not is not what he is describing.

Notice also where he puts each outcome: the benefit is **for** the one guided — "he only benefits himself"; the loss is **on** the one who strays — "against his own self." Ibn Kathir places both results squarely on the person concerned. Your guidance is your own; your straying is your own. Nobody carries either one for you.

## "And I am not set over you as a guardian"

The Prophet ﷺ is told to disclaim a role: in the Arabic, that of a *wakīl* — the word rendered here as "guardian." Ibn Kathir spells out precisely which role is being disclaimed: "I am not a guardian over you in order for you to become believers. **I am only a warner to you, and guidance belongs to Allah, the Exalted.**"

That is a short sentence carrying a large point of belief. Conveying and warning are the Messenger's ﷺ work; the guidance that actually makes someone a believer **belongs to Allah**. The Prophet ﷺ is not given the task of bringing anyone to faith, and is therefore not the one answerable for the refusals of those who heard him.

For anyone who carries this religion to others — a parent with a drifting child, a teacher, a friend who keeps trying — this half-ayah is a boundary marker, and a mercy. You are asked to be clear and to warn. You were not appointed *wakīl* over anyone's heart. Exhaustion and self-blame over another person's refusal are burdens the ayah lifts off you, because they were never assigned in the first place.

## Ayah 109: the two things that remain

With the outward announcement finished, the address narrows to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and gives him exactly two commands.

**"And follow what is revealed to you."** Ibn Kathir: "Adhere to that which Allah has revealed to you, and inspired you with." It is worth pausing on how striking this is. The one delivering the revelation is himself commanded to *follow* it. He stands under the message, not above it — which fits exactly with what he has just been told to say: he is a warner, not a *wakīl*.

**"And be patient."** Ibn Kathir does not leave patience as a vague virtue; he gives it a specific object: "be patient **with the opposition that you meet from the people**." This is not endurance of illness or poverty in general. It is the particular endurance of someone telling people the truth and being resisted for it. The command lands exactly where the weight of ayah 108 falls — on the Messenger ﷺ himself, who has delivered everything clearly and been met with refusal.

**"Until Allah gives judgment."** Ibn Kathir: "Until Allah judges between you and them." Look carefully at the endpoint the ayah sets. It is not "until they believe." It is not "until the opposition dies down." It is not "until you feel better." The horizon of the patience is **a decision that belongs to Allah**. That makes this patience something quite different from resignation: it is waiting inside a case that is certain to be judged.

**"And He is the best of the judges."** Ibn Kathir explains this with two qualities held together: He is the best of those who pass judgment "due to His Justice and His wisdom." Both halves matter to someone who has been told to wait. The ayah does not only say that the case will be decided; it says who will decide it, and describes Him as the best of those who decide — in justice, and in wisdom. That is what makes the waiting bearable: not the length of the wait, but the One at the end of it.

## The surah that ends "be patient" is the surah named for Yūnus

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting on the earlier part of this surah, gives long and careful attention to Sayyidnā Yūnus عليه السلام, and that account throws a particular light on the closing command.

His people lived at Nineveh, near Mosul in Iraq — more than a hundred thousand of them, as the Qur'an says. They refused to believe. Allah instructed Yūnus عليه السلام to warn them that the punishment would come within three days, and he announced it. Maʿārif is clear that his departure from the town that night was itself **by Divine command** — the same pattern seen with earlier communities, as with Sayyidnā Lūṭ عليه السلام, where Allah orders His messenger out of the area before the punishment falls.

What followed was not what he expected. His people, who had never known him to lie, saw the cloud-like black smoke gathering over them in the morning, went out to open ground with their women, children and animals, wearing rags, and wept and begged until the whole area rang with it. Allah accepted their repentance and lifted the punishment. Reports indicate this was ʿĀshūrāʾ, the tenth of Muḥarram.

Yūnus عليه السلام, waiting outside the town, knew none of this. When the punishment did not come, he faced a mortal danger: under the law of that people, a man proven a liar was killed. Maʿārif adds a line worth keeping: "The noble prophets are protected from every act of sin and disobedience, but are not set apart from others in terms of human nature and temperament." So he set out, reached the sea, and boarded a boat.

**Maʿārif is emphatic about what this was, and what it was not.** Prophets are *maʿṣūm* — Divinely protected from sin — and this is an uncontested belief on which the Ummah has consensus. Scholars have differed over details (whether the protection covers minor sins as well as major ones; whether it extends to the period before prophethood), but Maʿārif states that **no group and no individual has ever differed on this**: no prophet ever fell short in carrying out his mission, since there could be no greater sin for a prophet than falling short in the very mission for which Allah chose him. Accusations of that sort, Maʿārif shows, rest only on Israelite reports (*isrāʾīliyyāt*), which commentators agree are not authentic and on which no ruling of Islamic law may be based.

What did happen, as Maʿārif explains it, is that he boarded the boat intending to migrate **before Allah's permission had come** — no sin in itself, but different from the customary practice of the prophets, and not appropriate to the high station he had been given. That is what the Qur'an's words of displeasure address: *abaqa* in 37:140, a word used for a slave running away without his master's permission, and *dhahaba mughāḍiban* in 21:87. Tafsir Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, quoted by Maʿārif, puts it this way: he left "in anger against their bitter hostility and adamant infidelity despite that he had spent a long time as a prophet inviting them to faith. This journey of his was a kind of migration but he had not yet received the permission for it."

Then came the stalled boat, the lots drawn again and again, the fish waiting under Divine order with the instruction that this body was not her food but his home for a while — and, in that state, the words: *"There is no god but You. Pure are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers"* (21:87). Allah accepted the prayer and put him on the shore alive and unharmed, the heat having left no hair on his body, with a gourd vine grown near him for shade and a wild goat sent morning and evening so he could drink milk. Even the correction was wrapped in care.

Maʿārif does not itself connect that account to ayah 109. But the surah places them in one frame, and the reader can see the fit: **the surah named for the prophet whose slip was moving before his Lord's permission ends by telling the final Messenger ﷺ to follow the revelation and be patient *until Allah gives judgment*.** Not until the hostility eases. Until He decides.

## The door is still open — but it does not stay open

Ayah 108's "whoever is guided" is an invitation, and Maʿārif's discussion earlier in the surah tells us how long the invitation stands. **The door of repentance does not close even when a worldly punishment comes face to face.** It closes when the punishment of the Hereafter comes face to face — either on the Day of Qiyāmah, or at the time of death, whether natural death or death as the victim of some worldly punishment, as was the case with Pharaoh.

That is the difference between the people of Yūnus and Pharaoh. They repented when they *saw the punishment coming*, before it overtook them and before death; he declared belief only after the punishment had overtaken him, at the last rattle of death. Their repentance was accepted, his was not — and Maʿārif notes, quoting al-Qurtubi, that the account of Yūnus's people is placed in this surah immediately after Pharaoh's precisely so that the difference becomes clear.

Al-Qurtubi records genuine differences among the early authorities on how far the punishment had gone: **Ibn Jubayr** said it had covered them like the sheet of cloth on a grave, and Allah lifted it when their repentance turned out to be sound; **al-Ṭabarī** held that Yūnus's people were given a special place among all other peoples, their repentance accepted *after* they had seen the punishment, and he reports this from a large number of commentators; **al-Zajjāj** held that the punishment had not yet fallen on them at all — they had only seen the signs that proved it was coming, and had they seen the punishment itself falling upon them, their believing would have been no good to them. Al-Qurtubi judged al-Zajjāj's view the better one, since the sight after which repentance is not accepted is the one in which a person is actually seized — as happened with Pharaoh. He supports it with a saying of the Prophet ﷺ — that Allah accepts the repentance of a servant until he is rattled by death, *al-ghargharah* being the rattling sound that comes from the throat when death takes hold. (The source quotes this saying without naming a collection.) A narration from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه carries the same sense: they repented before the punishment actually fell.

So ayah 108 is an open door with a closing time. The truth "has surely come"; the choosing is genuinely yours; and the window in which choosing counts is the window before the rattle.

## Living it

**If you are the one hearing:** the ayah gives you the dignity of a real choice and the weight of a real account. Guidance benefits you; straying costs you. And Ibn Kathir's phrasing — guided *and* following — means the response the ayah is after is not agreement but practice.

**If you are the one conveying:** say it clearly, warn honestly, and then stop where the ayah stops you. You are not *wakīl*. Guidance belongs to Allah. Refusal by the people you love is not proof that you failed and not a load you were given to carry.

**When it costs you:** ayah 109 names the two duties in order — first *follow what is revealed*, then *be patient*. Endurance without adherence is just stubbornness; adherence without endurance does not survive the first serious opposition. Both, together.

**When you want it resolved now:** the endpoint the ayah sets is *ḥattā yaḥkuma Allāh* — until Allah judges. And its last words are the reason waiting is not a loss: **He is the best of judges**, in His justice and in His wisdom.
